narration:
This part adds noise to the autoencoder during training, on top of the variational setup that already shapes the latent space. It uses two kinds of dropout. Each one has a rate of zero point one five.

The first kind acts on the latent vector. Before the latent vector goes into the decoder, randomly drop some of its entries at that rate. The decoder therefore never sees a complete vector, and it can't depend on any single dimension. The autoencoder has to spread the information redundantly across dimensions. That makes it tolerant of small prediction errors from the generative model that will later produce these vectors.

The second kind acts on the input. Before the encoder reads a chunk of tokens, randomly mask a fraction of the tokens, again at a rate of zero point one five. The decoder must still reconstruct the full chunk. So the autoencoder has to infer the masked tokens from the tokens around them. This is like the Continuous Bag-of-Words method from word embeddings. The effect is that the latent vector carries the semantic context of the chunk, rather than being a plain compression of token indices.

Both dropouts apply only while training the autoencoder. Turn them off when you later train the continuous language model and when you run inference.

Now the setup this gives. A chunk is four tokens, and the latent vector has one hundred twenty-eight dimensions. That size leaves room to store information redundantly. The encoder outputs a mean and a standard deviation for each dimension, and the latent vector is sampled from that distribution. During training the standard deviations settle at about zero point three. So sampling adds substantial Gaussian noise to the predicted mean, with a standard deviation of about zero point three in every dimension.

Even with that much noise, the decoder reconstructs tokens with accuracy above ninety-nine point nine percent. The result is a representation that is both faithful and robust. It is the foundation for learning the continuous autoregressive language model, which the paper calls CALM.

This part covers where the training targets come from. In this method, a target is the representation of a block of the image, not the pixels of that block.

There are four steps.

First, take the input image, which the paper calls y, and cut it into non-overlapping patches. The paper calls the number of patches N. The patches form a sequence, in order.

Second, feed that whole patch sequence through the target encoder. The paper marks its parameters with a bar over the parameter symbol. The target for a block is the set of target encoder outputs at exactly the patches in its mask. So you simply look up the stored vectors at those positions. One detail matters a lot. You mask the output of the target encoder, not the input image. The whole image goes through the encoder first, and only afterwards do you pick out the blocks. The paper says this is crucial for making the targets high level and semantic.

Then remove from it any region covered by the target blocks. This leaves a context that is informative yet sparse, so it is cheap to process, while the targets stay relatively semantic.

narration:
Here is the problem this part solves. Temperature sampling normally means rescaling the logits before the softmax. That needs the model's probabilities. In this framework the generative head is likelihood-free. It gives you a sampler and nothing else. So we need temperature sampling from a black-box sampler, and the paper gives an exact algorithm for it, built on rejection sampling.

One sample here is a whole chunk of tokens, produced in one step. Call that chunk x, and call its probability under the sampler P of x.

Start with the easy case. The temperature is one divided by a whole number n. The target distribution is then proportional to P of x raised to the power n. The chance of drawing the same chunk in n independent draws is also P of x to the power n. So the scheme is simple. Draw n samples. If all n are identical, accept that chunk. Otherwise throw the whole set away and start again.

Now the general case, for a temperature strictly between zero and one. Work with the inverse temperature, one divided by the temperature. Split it into two parts. The whole part, which the paper calls n, is its floor. The fractional part, which the paper calls alpha, is the inverse temperature minus n. This gives a two-stage procedure.

Stage one handles the whole part. Draw n independent samples. If they are not all identical, reject and restart. If they are, the shared chunk becomes the candidate.

Stage two handles the fractional part. Here the paper draws on Bernoulli Factory theory. It builds an iterative procedure that simulates a biased coin, whose chance of success is P of the candidate raised to the power alpha. I can't give you the inner loop of that procedure from this description. Treat it as a black box and take its exact steps from the paper's first algorithm. If the coin succeeds, the candidate is accepted. When the inverse temperature is a whole number, alpha is zero, so this stage is skipped and you are back in the easy case.

A chunk is accepted only if it passes both stages. A failure at any point restarts everything from stage one.

The paper's first theorem says this algorithm is exact. Accepted samples have probability proportional to P of x raised to the inverse temperature. The normalizer is the sum of that quantity over all possible chunks. The proof is in the appendix.

The prediction step takes what the context encoder produced and uses it to guess the representations of the target blocks. There are several target blocks, and each one has its own representation that we want to predict. The paper writes the number of target blocks as M.

Each target block comes with a target mask. This is simply the list of patch locations that belong to that block.

The predictor is a learned network with its own parameters. It runs once per target block. Here is what one run looks like, in three parts.

First, build the inputs. One input is the output of the context encoder. The other input is a set of mask tokens, one for every patch location in this target block.

Second, make the mask tokens. Start with a single learnable vector that is shared by all mask tokens. For each location in the block, add the positional embedding for that location to this shared vector. So each mask token is tied to the patch it stands for.

Third, run the predictor. It takes the context encoder output together with the mask tokens for this block. It returns one predicted representation for each patch in the block. That is a patch-level prediction, with one output per mask token.

Now repeat this for every target block. Each time, keep the same context encoder output, but swap in the mask tokens for that block's locations. The predictor's weights and the shared mask vector stay the same across all runs.

The result is one set of predicted patch representations per target block. The number of prediction sets therefore equals the number of target blocks.

Start with the obvious way to evaluate this model. You run next-token prediction in a teacher-forcing setting. At each step the model produces two latent vectors. You decode them with the decoder of the frozen autoencoder. Then you compute the Brier score using only the first token of each decoded chunk.

That check is not enough. It ignores the quality of every other token in the chunk. If the chunk size is K, that leaves K minus one tokens that never get scored.

So the paper introduces Brier-n, a version of the Brier score computed over whole n-grams. In the estimator, the indicator functions treat the entire n-gram as a single atomic outcome, rather than a single token.

Next, you need one number to report. The paper follows the convention of established n-gram metrics such as bleu, and builds a composite called BrierLM, short for Brier for Language Modeling. It works in three steps.

First, compute Brier-n for n equal to one, two, three and four. That gives four scores.

Second, multiply the four scores together and take the result to the power of one quarter. This is the geometric mean.

Third, multiply by one hundred. The scaling puts the metric on a more interpretable range from zero to one hundred.

narration:
The Brier score is a sound way to judge a predicted distribution, but there is a catch. Computing it directly needs the full predictive distribution, which the paper calls P. For the model called CALM, that distribution is out of reach. All we can do is draw samples from the model. So the trick is to estimate the score from samples alone, with no likelihoods, and still get an unbiased answer.

The score has two pieces, and each gets its own estimator. Then they are combined.

First, the uncertainty term. This is the sum, over all possible outcomes, of the squared probability of each outcome. Read it differently: it is the chance that two independent samples from the model land on the same outcome. That is a collision probability. So an unbiased estimate is simple. Draw two independent samples from the model. Score one if they are equal, and zero otherwise.

Second, the accuracy term. This is the probability the model gives to the true outcome, which the paper calls y. Draw one sample from the model. Score one if it equals the true outcome, and zero otherwise. The average of that indicator is exactly the probability of the true outcome, so it is also unbiased.

Now put it together. You need only two independent samples from the model, call them the first sample and the second sample. Compute three indicators. The first is one if the first sample equals the true outcome. The second is one if the second sample equals the true outcome. The third is one if the two samples equal each other. The Brier estimate is the first indicator plus the second, minus the third.

Because each piece is unbiased, the combined estimate is unbiased too. That means CALM's predictive quality can be evaluated without ever computing a likelihood.

The setup is two numbers. Take one over T and round it down to a whole number. The paper calls that n. Then subtract n from one over T to get the fractional part, which the paper calls alpha.

Once you have a candidate, check alpha. If alpha is zero, one over T was a whole number. Return the candidate immediately.

Otherwise, go on to stage two, which handles the fractional part. Start a counter at one. Then loop.

In each pass, draw one new sample from the base sampler. If it equals the candidate, return the candidate and stop. If it differs, draw a uniform random number between zero and one. The generative head is built from a stack of residual blocks, each one a multilayer perceptron block. The paper calls the number of blocks capital L, and I'll call it the block count.

The stack starts from the noise, which the paper calls epsilon. The first representation is set equal to this noise. Each block then refines the current representation, so the stack progressively turns the noise into the final output vector.

Each block does three things, in order.

This part covers the training loss of I-JEPA, and it is simple. Training works on one comparison: what the predictor outputs against what the target encoder produces.

Here is what goes in. For each target block, there is a predicted representation for every patch in that block, coming from the predictor. There is also a target representation for every one of those patches, coming from the target encoder. Both are vectors, one per patch.

The loss has three steps.

First, for one patch, subtract the target vector from the predicted vector. Square each entry of that difference and add them up. That gives the squared Euclidean distance for the patch.

Second, for one target block, do that for every patch in the block and add the results together. So a block's distance is a sum over its patches, not an average.

Third, do this for every target block. The paper calls the number of target blocks M. Add up the block distances and divide by M. That average is the loss.

Now, what gets trained. The predictor, whose parameters the paper calls phi, is learned by gradient-based optimization. So is the context encoder, whose parameters the paper calls theta.

The target encoder is different. Its parameters are not learned by gradients. Instead, they are updated as an exponential moving average of the context encoder's parameters.

Why build it this way? An exponential moving average target encoder has proven essential for training joint-embedding architectures with Vision Transformers. The authors find the same is true for I-JEPA.

narration:
The first piece of the framework, which the paper calls CALM, is an autoencoder. Its job is to learn a one-to-one mapping between a chunk of discrete tokens and a single continuous vector. The encoder takes a chunk of tokens from the vocabulary and produces the vector. The decoder takes that vector and returns a chunk of tokens from the vocabulary. The number of tokens in a chunk is the chunk size, which the paper calls K. The length of the vector is the latent dimension, which the paper calls l. The goal is simple: decode the encoding of a chunk, and get the original tokens back.

One design choice first. The autoencoder is context-free. It handles each chunk on its own, without looking at the rest of the sequence. That keeps it simple and cheap. A version that also conditions on earlier vectors is left for future work.

The encoder has four steps. One, look up an embedding for each token, so you have one per token in the chunk. Two, pass each embedding separately through the same feed-forward network. Three, flatten the resulting hidden states into one long vector, of size chunk size times the hidden dimension, and apply a linear layer that compresses it down to the hidden dimension, which the paper calls d. Four, pass that through a second feed-forward network, then a linear projection down to the latent dimension. That output is the latent vector.

The decoder mirrors this, also in four steps. One, apply a linear layer and a feed-forward network to the latent vector, giving a hidden state of the hidden dimension. Two, apply another linear layer that expands it to chunk size times hidden dimension, and reshape that into one hidden state per token position. Three, pass each state through a second feed-forward network, then project to vocabulary logits using the input embedding matrix, the very same one the encoder uses. Four, take the argmax over the logits at each position to get the tokens.

Training uses plain cross-entropy. For each position in the chunk, take the log probability the decoder gives to the true token, given the latent vector from encoding the chunk. Sum those and negate.

The authors validate this architecture empirically and find it both highly effective and efficient. With a chunk size of four, a latent dimension of just ten is enough, giving token accuracy above ninety-nine point nine percent. The hidden dimension is five hundred twelve, and the network is shallow. Its cost is almost negligible next to the language model.

narration:
This procedure draws one sample that roughly follows a sharpened version of a base sampler's distribution. Each item's probability is raised to a power, then renormalized. The paper calls that power n, and the target temperature is one divided by n.

It takes three inputs. The first is the base sampler, which you can draw samples from. The second is the power n. The third is a batch size, which the paper calls capital N. The batch size must be much larger than the power. The output is a single sample whose probability is approximately proportional to its base probability raised to the power n.

There are three steps.

First, draw a batch from the base sampler, as many samples as the batch size.

Second, count how many times each unique sample appears in the batch. Keep one count per unique sample.

Third, run a loop over a trial value, which the paper calls m. Start m at n and step it down by one each pass, until it reaches one. Each pass does the following. Make an empty candidate set and an empty list of weights. Go through every unique sample whose count is at least m. Add that sample to the candidate set. Add a weight to the list equal to the number of ways to choose m items from that sample's count. That is the combinations number, count choose m. After going through all the samples, check the candidate set. If it is not empty, stop the loop, because you have a valid candidate set. If it is empty, reduce m by one and try again. The fallback matters when no sample appears n times in the batch. A smaller m then lets some sample qualify. When m reaches one, every sample in the batch qualifies, so the set cannot be empty.

Finally, pick one sample from the candidate set, with probability proportional to its weight, and return it.

This procedure is not exact for a fixed batch. For any finite batch size, which the paper calls N, the output distribution is biased. It does not quite match the target distribution you wanted to sample from.

The reason is where the final probability comes from. The chance of returning a particular sample is set by a ratio of weights, and those weights are computed inside a single random batch. Each batch is a fresh random draw, so the ratio is itself random.

Exactness would need the average of that ratio over many batches to equal the ratio of the averages. It generally does not. The expectation of a ratio is not the ratio of expectations. That gap is the bias.

The bias does not last forever, though. The algorithm is asymptotically unbiased. As the batch size grows toward infinity, the output distribution converges to the true target distribution.

The authors call this property crucial, and they state it formally in the theorem that comes next.

The theorem is about whether Algorithm two samples from the right distribution. Here is what it says.

Run Algorithm two with some batch size. The paper calls the batch size N. Now ask how likely the algorithm is to return one particular item. That chance is the algorithm's sampling probability for that item, and it depends on the batch size.

Next, define what we actually want. The target is the model's probability of the item, raised to a power, then divided by a normalizing constant. The paper calls that power n. It is the inverse of the temperature, so the temperature, which the paper calls T, equals one divided by n.

The normalizing constant is a sum. For every possible item, take the model's probability, raise it to that same power, and add them all up. Dividing by this sum makes the target probabilities add up to one.

So the target is a proper distribution. It is the model's own distribution, sharpened or flattened by the temperature.

The theorem then makes one claim. As the batch size grows without bound, the algorithm's probability of returning any given item converges to the target probability of that item. That convergence is what the authors mean by saying the algorithm is asymptotically unbiased.

The proof is in the appendix.

The authors call this property consistency, and they say it makes the algorithm a principled approximation. It also gives the batch size a role in practice. The batch size is a lever for trading off efficiency against accuracy, and you choose it with that tradeoff in mind.

The algorithm relies only on a black-box sampling interface. That means it needs nothing from the model except the ability to draw samples from it.

Because of this, its usefulness goes beyond the CALM framework. It applies naturally to the whole class of implicit language models.

The authors therefore describe it as a universal toolkit for controlled decoding in discrete spaces.

narration:
The exact algorithm struggles when used at low temperatures. At these temperatures, it needs to draw many identical samples, which causes a high rejection rate and wastes samples. To fix this, an approximate algorithm is introduced for low temperatures of the form T equals one over n. The value of n is the floor of one over T, not just one over T. 

The main idea is to move from a single, high-risk trial to a combinatorial search within a large batch of N samples, where N is much larger than n. This change allows one batch to contain many different candidates, specifically the number of ways to choose n from N, improving sample use and increasing the chance of finding a successful match in one round.

For example, when sampling at T equals one half, which means n equals two, a batch of N equals ten samples might be drawn, like A, C, A, D, B, E, A, F, B, G. In this example, sample A appears three times, and sample B appears two times. The algorithm counts how many successful n-tuple candidates are in the batch for each sample using the number of ways to choose n from the count of times the sample appears.

For sample A, there are three successful candidates because the number of ways to choose two from three is three. For sample B, there is one successful candidate because the number of ways to choose two from two is one. The output is chosen from the valid candidates A and B based on their weighted probabilities. In this example, the probability of choosing A is three over four, and the probability of choosing B is one over four.

If no sample appears at least n times, the candidate set would be empty. To ensure the algorithm always produces an output, a fallback mechanism is introduced. The fallback mechanism reduces the matching requirement from n to n minus one, then n minus two, and so on, until a non-empty candidate set is found. This ensures the algorithm always produces an output, even in rare cases where no sample meets the initial requirement.

The algorithm starts by drawing a large batch of samples from the base sampler. This batch size is much larger than the target temperature’s denominator, n. Each sample in the batch is counted to see how many times it appears.  

Next, the algorithm checks for samples that appear at least n times in the batch. It begins with the target value of n and works downward if needed. For each m from n down to 1, it reinitializes the candidate set and the weights list. For each unique sample that appears at least m times, it adds the sample to the candidate set and calculates a weight using a combination formula. This weight represents how many ways the sample could have appeared m times in the batch.  

If the candidate set is not empty for the current m, the algorithm stops checking lower values and moves forward. The final step is to choose a sample from the candidate set, with the probability of each sample being proportional to its weight. This ensures the output sample follows the desired distribution, where each sample’s probability is proportional to the base sampler’s probability raised to the power of n.  

The fallback mechanism ensures the algorithm always produces an output, even if no sample meets the initial requirement. By reducing the count requirement step by step, it finds a valid candidate set. This makes the algorithm robust and reliable for generating samples that approximate the target distribution.

The algorithm has bias when using any finite batch size. This happens because the output probability is calculated using the ratio of weights from a single stochastic batch. The expectation of a ratio is usually not the same as the ratio of expectations. This mismatch introduces bias into the results. However, the algorithm's main advantage is that it becomes unbiased as the batch size grows infinitely large. As the batch size approaches infinity, the output distribution gets closer to the true target distribution. This important property is stated formally in a theorem. The theorem shows that the algorithm's output converges to the correct distribution as more data is used. This makes the method reliable for large-scale applications. The bias is a limitation when working with small batches, but it fades away as more samples are included. This property ensures that the algorithm can be trusted when enough data is available. The theorem provides a mathematical guarantee for this behavior. The algorithm balances accuracy and efficiency by allowing practical use with finite batches while ensuring correctness in the limit.

The theorem introduces two key probability distributions. The first is the probability of sampling x using Algorithm 2 with a batch size of N. The second is a target distribution defined as P(x) raised to the power of n, divided by a normalization factor. This normalization factor is the sum of P(x) raised to the power of n for all possible x. The temperature in this target distribution is the reciprocal of n. As the batch size N grows toward infinity, the probability from Algorithm 2 gets closer to this target distribution. This means the algorithm becomes more accurate as N increases. The proof of this result is in Appendix A.3. The theorem shows the algorithm is consistent, making it a principled way to approximate the target distribution. The batch size N controls the tradeoff between efficiency and accuracy. With larger N, the algorithm becomes more precise but uses more resources. With smaller N, it runs faster but is less accurate. This gives users a way to adjust performance based on their needs. The theorem ensures that even with finite batches, the algorithm remains a valid approximation. As N increases, the approximation improves. This makes the algorithm both practical and theoretically sound. The consistency property is key to its reliability. The theorem confirms that the method works as intended in the limit, giving confidence in its use. The temperature is directly tied to n, with no need for rounding or flooring. The value of n is simply one divided by the temperature.

The algorithm uses a black-box sampling interface, meaning it doesn’t need to know the model’s internal details. This makes it compatible with more than just the CALM framework. It can work with all implicit language models. The approach acts as a universal toolkit for controlled decoding in discrete spaces. The design avoids assumptions about the model’s structure, letting it adapt to different systems. This flexibility means it can be applied widely. The method doesn’t require special modifications to the model. It uses standard sampling procedures. This keeps the implementation simple. The result is a general-purpose tool for guiding outputs in discrete settings. The approach is not limited to specific model types. It works wherever a sampling interface is available.

To fix this, the paper proposes an approximate algorithm for low temperatures, where the temperature is one divided by a whole number. Using a large batch of samples allows for many candidates, improving sample use and increasing the chance of finding a match in one go. This shift works best when the batch size is much larger than the number needed. A single batch can then form a specific combinatorial value of choosing a certain number of samples from the batch. For example, at a temperature of one half, which means the number needed is two, a batch of ten samples might be drawn, like a set containing letters such as A, C, A, D, B, E, A, F, B, and G. This mechanism reduces the matching requirement from two to one, then to zero, and so on, until a non-empty candidate set is found. The exact algorithm requires drawing a number of identical samples equal to the floor of one divided by the temperature, not just one divided by the temperature.

The algorithm is called Approximate Temperature Sampling. It generates a sample that approximates a specific distribution. It takes as input a base sampler, a target temperature defined as one divided by n, and a batch size N that is much larger than n. The output is a sample that approximates the distribution where the probability of each sample is proportional to the base sampler's probability raised to the power of n. 

The algorithm starts by drawing a batch of N samples from the base sampler. It then counts how many times each unique sample appears in the batch. Next, it enters a loop that starts with the value n and decrements down to one. In each iteration of the loop, it creates a candidate set of samples that appear at least as many times as the current loop value. For each sample in the candidate set, it calculates a weight that represents the number of combinations of samples that could produce the current sample using the binomial coefficient. 

If the candidate set is not empty, the loop stops and proceeds to the next step. The algorithm then selects a sample from the candidate set, with the probability of each sample being proportional to its weight. The selected sample is returned as the output of the algorithm. 

This approach allows the algorithm to find a valid candidate set even if the initial batch does not contain enough identical samples. By reducing the required number of identical samples in each iteration, the algorithm increases the chances of finding a suitable candidate. The use of binomial coefficients ensures that the weights accurately reflect the number of combinations that could lead to each sample. This method efficiently approximates the desired distribution without requiring an exact match for the target temperature.

narration:
The model starts with discrete tokens instead of using compact latent vectors as input. This is because the model had trouble learning from those small vectors. So, the input is built from K tokens from the previous step. These tokens are embedded and then compressed into a single input using a two-layer MLP. This keeps things efficient while still giving the model enough information to work with.

During inference, at each step, the model takes the last K tokens it generated. It embeds them and runs them through the compression module to get a single input representation. This is fed into the Transformer. The Transformer then outputs a hidden state. This hidden state is used by an energy-based generative head to predict the next continuous vector.

Once the continuous vector is predicted, it’s passed through the frozen decoder of a pre-trained autoencoder. This decoder turns the continuous vector back into K discrete tokens. These tokens become the input for the next step. This creates a loop between the continuous and discrete representations. The model uses this loop to generate new tokens step by step.

This setup helps the model stay grounded in the discrete token space, which is where the original data lives. The compression module ensures that the input is manageable, and the autoencoder helps convert predictions back into tokens. This way, the model can generate new tokens without losing the discrete structure of the original data.

narration: The generative head is built from a stack of L residual MLP blocks. These blocks take an initial noise vector called epsilon zero and gradually turn it into the final output. The first step in each block is to combine the current representation with a hidden state using two linear layers. This helps the model learn complex patterns in the data. Next, a SwiGLU layer is applied. This layer has an intermediate dimension of d, which controls how much information is processed at each step. After that, a residual connection is added. This means the input to the block is added back to the output, helping the model train more effectively. Finally, a linear layer transforms the representation into the target dimension l. This gives the final output vector, called Z sub i. The whole process allows the model to refine the initial noise into a meaningful output. The residual connections help the model keep track of important features as it processes the data. The SwiGLU layer adds non-linearity, letting the model capture more complex relationships. The linear layer at the end ensures the output has the right shape for whatever task the model is doing. Each block in the stack builds on the previous one, making the output more refined with every step. This design lets the model handle intricate transformations while staying stable during training.

narration:
The paper introduces two dropout methods to make the autoencoder's latent space more robust. First, during training, a dropout rate of fifteen percent is applied to the latent vector before it goes to the decoder. This forces the model to learn a representation that can handle small errors from the generative model downstream. 

Second, the same dropout rate is used on the input tokens. Some tokens are randomly masked, and the model must predict them based on the surrounding context. This is similar to the CBOW method, where the model learns from the context of words rather than just their positions. This helps the latent vector capture the meaning of the chunk, not just the token indexes.

These dropout techniques are only used during the autoencoder's training. Once the model moves on to training and using the continuous language model, the dropout is turned off. This ensures the model can rely on the robust latent space it learned.

For a chunk of four tokens, the latent vector has one hundred twenty-eight dimensions. This size gives the model enough capacity to encode information redundantly. The encoder learns a posterior distribution where the standard deviations settle around point three. This means that when sampling the latent vector, it adds noise that's about point three times the identity matrix. This is a significant amount of noise, but the decoder still manages to keep a token-level accuracy above ninety-nine point nine percent. 

This combination of high accuracy and robustness creates a strong foundation for the next step, which is training the Continuous Autoregressive Language Model, or CALM.

narration:
The CALM framework starts with an autoencoder that learns to map a sequence of K discrete tokens to a continuous vector and back. This autoencoder has two parts: an encoder that turns tokens into vectors and a decoder that turns vectors back into tokens. The encoder processes each token chunk independently, without looking at the surrounding sequence. A version that uses previous vectors is something to explore later.

The encoder begins by turning each token into an embedding. Each embedding goes through a position-wise feed-forward network. The K hidden states from this are flattened and compressed by a linear layer, reducing the dimension from Kd to d. This compressed representation goes through another feed-forward network and a linear projection to create the l-dimensional latent vector z.

The decoder takes z and first transforms it using a linear layer and a feed-forward network to get a d-dimensional hidden state. This hidden state is expanded by a separate linear layer to Kd dimensions and reshaped into a sequence of K hidden states. Each of these states goes through a second feed-forward network and is projected to vocabulary logits using the same embedding matrix used for the encoder. The tokens are then reconstructed by picking the most probable token at each position using an argmax operation.

The autoencoder is trained by minimizing the reconstruction error using a cross-entropy loss over all K tokens. This loss is the negative sum of the log probabilities of each token given the latent vector from the encoder. In testing, this setup works well. For example, with K equal to four tokens and a latent vector of ten dimensions, the model achieves over ninety-nine point nine percent accuracy. The autoencoder is simple, with a hidden dimension of five hundred twelve, and it doesn’t add much computational cost compared to a language model.

narration: The problem the paper calls posterior collapse happens in variational autoencoders, or VAEs. Some parts of the model's hidden representation stop being useful for reconstructing the input data. When a hidden part collapses, it stops carrying meaningful information about the input. These collapsed parts still follow the standard normal distribution but do not help with reconstruction. They add random noise that makes training a language model using the VAE's output more difficult. The noise from collapsed parts makes the training process unstable. To solve this, the authors use a method called KL clipping, introduced by Kingma et al. in two thousand and sixteen. KL clipping changes the way the model's loss is calculated during training. Instead of allowing the KL divergence for each hidden part to be as low as possible, the method sets a minimum value for it. This minimum value is called a threshold and is set to one half in this case. The KL divergence for each hidden part is compared to this threshold. If the KL divergence is lower than the threshold, the threshold value is used instead. This ensures that each hidden part contributes meaningfully to the reconstruction of the input data. By using this method, the model avoids posterior collapse. The method encourages the model to use all parts of the hidden representation in a structured and meaningful way. The threshold value of one half ensures that each dimension is encouraged to actively participate in reconstruction, thus preventing collapse and fostering a dense, structured representation. Each dimension’s KL divergence is clipped separately before summing them. This way, every part of the hidden representation is pushed to carry meaningful information, not just the total.

narration:
The goal is to sample from a distribution with a given temperature, but the model only gives a black-box sampler. This means we can’t directly adjust probabilities—we need a workaround. The idea is to use rejection sampling, a method that lets us indirectly shape the distribution by accepting or rejecting samples based on certain rules. 

The core idea comes from the observation that repeating a sampling process can simulate raising probabilities to a power. For example, if you want to sample from a distribution where each probability is raised to the power of n, you can draw n samples and accept them only if they are all the same. This works because the chance of getting the same sample n times is exactly the probability raised to the power of n. 

For a temperature that is the reciprocal of an integer, this method gives the right distribution. But to handle any temperature between zero and one, we break it into two parts: an integer part and a fractional part. The integer part uses the repetition trick described. The fractional part is more complex. It uses a technique from Bernoulli Factory theory, which lets us simulate a biased coin flip with a success probability equal to the probability of a sample raised to the fractional power. 

The algorithm runs in two stages. First, it handles the integer part by repeating the sampling process and checking for identical results. If that fails, it restarts. If it passes, it moves to the second stage, where it simulates the fractional part using the Bernoulli Factory method. Only if both stages succeed is the sample accepted. If either stage fails, the whole process starts over. 

This ensures that the final samples follow the desired temperature-adjusted distribution. The math checks out, and the proof is in the appendix. The method is exact, meaning it perfectly matches the target distribution, even though it uses only a black-box sampler.

narration:
The component Brier-n extends the original Brier score to evaluate how well a model predicts sequences of tokens, not just single tokens. It works by treating each group of n consecutive tokens, called an n-gram, as a single outcome. The method starts by generating two latent vectors at each step, which are then decoded using a frozen autoencoder’s decoder. This gives two sequences of tokens. The original approach only looked at the first token of each sequence, but Brier-n looks at the entire sequence. 

The Brier score is calculated for each n-gram, treating the whole group as one event. This means the model is judged on how accurately it predicts the entire n-gram, not just the first token. The authors chose this approach because it better reflects real-world language use, where sequences of tokens are more meaningful than single tokens. 

To compute the score, the method uses indicator functions that treat the n-gram as a single, atomic outcome. This means the model’s prediction for the whole n-gram is compared to the actual n-gram in one step, rather than checking each token separately. 

To create a composite metric, the Brier-n scores for n equals one through four are combined using a geometric mean. This gives a single score that balances the performance across different sequence lengths. The final score is scaled by multiplying it by one hundred, so it falls on a zero to one hundred range, making it easier to interpret. The formula for BrierLM is one hundred times the fourth root of the product of the four Brier-n scores. This ensures that each n-gram length contributes equally to the final score. The algorithm is called likelihood-free temperature sampling. It lets you sample from a distribution at a given temperature. You start with a base sampler for an implicit discrete distribution and a target temperature between zero and one. The output is a sample accepted with a probability proportional to the original distribution raised to the power of one over the temperature.  

The algorithm has two stages. The first handles the integer part of the reciprocal of the temperature. The second handles the fractional part.  

To find the integer part, take the floor of the reciprocal of the temperature. Then draw that many independent and identically distributed samples from the base sampler. If all the samples are the same, keep that one as the result of this stage. If they are not, restart from the beginning of this stage.  

If the fractional part is zero, return the result from the integer part stage as the final sample.  

For the fractional part, start with a counter set to one. Then repeatedly draw a sample from the base sampler. If it matches the result from the integer part stage, return that sample as the final result.  

If it doesn’t match, draw a uniform random number between zero and one. If the number is less than the fractional part divided by the counter, restart from the beginning of the integer part stage. If not, increase the counter by one and continue the loop.  

This method lets you adjust the temperature without needing the likelihood. It works by using the base sampler repeatedly and adjusting the acceptance probability based on the temperature. The integer and fractional parts handle the scaling in a way that avoids direct computation of the likelihood.

The energy loss is a training objective built using the energy score, which measures alignment between predictions and observations through sample distances instead of probability densities. It compares a predictive distribution P with a ground truth observation y by calculating the expected distance between samples from P and between samples from P and y. The energy score is defined as the expected distance between two samples from P minus twice the expected distance between a sample from P and the ground truth y. This score is strictly proper for any alpha between zero and two, and alpha is typically set to one. The first part of the score encourages diversity in the model's predictions by penalizing identical samples. The second part encourages fidelity by pushing predictions closer to the ground truth. 

The exact computation of the energy score is intractable, so an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator is used as a practical loss function called the energy loss. To compute the energy loss, eight candidate samples are drawn from the generative head at each step. The autoencoder maps a token chunk to a conditional Gaussian posterior instead of a fixed point. Using a single sample as ground truth can introduce high variance, so one hundred target samples are drawn from the posterior to reduce this variance. The final energy loss combines the candidate samples and the target samples to calculate the loss. The energy loss formula subtracts the average distance between candidate samples from twice the average distance between target and candidate samples. 

The number of model samples affects training cost, so a small number is used for efficiency. Drawing target vectors from a known Gaussian posterior has negligible overhead, allowing for a large number of target samples to reduce loss variance. The energy loss is advantageous because it is likelihood-free, requiring only the ability to draw samples from the generative head. This flexibility allows minimal constraints on the internal architecture of the generative head, enabling simple and efficient designs.

The paper introduces variational regularization as a way to build a smoother latent space. Instead of using a regular autoencoder that maps inputs directly to a fixed latent vector, the encoder now outputs parameters of a diagonal Gaussian distribution. These parameters are called mu and sigma. The latent vector z is no longer fixed but is sampled from this Gaussian distribution. This introduces randomness into the encoding process.  

A new term is added to the loss function. It's called the KL divergence loss. This measures how much the encoded distribution differs from a standard normal distribution, which has zero mean and identity covariance. The loss function is a weighted sum of two parts: the reconstruction loss, which measures how well the model can recreate the input, and the KL divergence loss.  

The weight between these two parts is controlled by a hyperparameter called beta. The paper sets beta to one thousandth. This means the regularization term has a small influence compared to the reconstruction loss.  

The KL divergence is calculated using a specific formula. It involves summing terms that include the square of sigma and the square of mu for each dimension. These terms are combined with logarithms and constants. The formula includes a negative sign in front of the sum, ensuring that the encoded distribution stays close to the standard normal prior.  

This approach prevents the encoder from using overly precise or large values in the latent space. The result is a latent manifold that is smoother and more structured. This makes it easier to use for generative modeling, where the model needs to generate new data points from the latent space. The method aligns with other prominent generative models that also use smooth latent spaces.

The predicted representations come from the predictor and context encoder. Their parameters are learned using gradient-based optimization. The target encoder has its own parameters, but they are not learned the same way. Instead, they are updated using an exponential moving average of the context-encoder parameters. This means the target encoder’s parameters slowly follow the context encoder’s parameters over time. 

This approach is important for training JEAs with Vision Transformers. It helps stabilize the learning process and ensures the target encoder stays aligned with the context encoder. The same method works well for I-JEPA. 

The exponential moving average is a smooth way to update the target encoder. It avoids sudden changes that could disrupt learning. The moving average uses a weighted average of past context encoder parameters, with more weight on recent values. This keeps the target encoder consistent while allowing it to adapt gradually.

Posterior collapse is a problem that happens in variational autoencoders, or VAEs. It occurs when some parts of the model's hidden representation stop being useful for reconstructing the input data. When a part of the model collapses, it stops carrying meaningful information about the input. These collapsed parts act like random noise, which can make training other parts of the model, like a language model, less stable.  

To prevent this, the authors use a method called KL clipping. This method changes the training objective by setting a minimum value for the KL divergence loss of each part of the model. The minimum value is a constant floor, and it is applied to each dimension of the model's hidden representation.  

The formula for the clipped KL divergence loss adds up the maximum between the minimum value and the actual KL divergence loss for each dimension. The minimum value used in the formula is called lambda KL, and the authors set it to one half. This ensures that each part of the model's hidden representation contributes to the reconstruction of the input data.  

By using this method, the model avoids posterior collapse and creates a more useful and structured hidden representation. Every dimension is encouraged to actively participate in reconstruction, which prevents collapse and fosters a dense, structured representation. This technique helps stabilize the training process and ensures that all parts of the model carry meaningful information.

The model starts with discrete tokens instead of latent vectors. The first idea was to take the previous latent vectors and project them into the Transformer’s hidden space using a linear layer. But this didn’t work well. The model had trouble learning from those compressed inputs. So they changed the approach.  

Now, the model uses discrete tokens directly. During training, the input for each step comes from the K tokens generated in the previous step. To keep things efficient, they use a two-layer MLP as a compression module. This takes the K token embeddings and squishes them into one single input vector.  

At inference, step by step, the model takes the last K tokens generated. These are embedded and run through the same compression module. The output is fed into the Transformer. The Transformer returns a hidden state. This hidden state is used by the energy-based generative head to predict the next continuous vector.  

Once the continuous vector is predicted, it goes through the frozen decoder of a pre-trained autoencoder. This decoder turns the vector back into K discrete tokens. These tokens become the input for the next step.  

This setup lets the model work with discrete tokens throughout the process. The compression module keeps things efficient, and the autoencoder ensures the model stays aligned with the discrete token space. The whole system is called CALM, and its design is shown in Figure 2.

The second method applies the same dropout rate to the input tokens, randomly masking fifteen percent of them. Both methods are used only during training and are turned off during inference. The autoencoder processes chunks of four tokens and uses a latent vector of one hundred twenty-eight dimensions. The encoder learns a posterior distribution where the standard deviations converge to approximately zero point three. This means that when sampling the latent vector, the predicted mean is perturbed by Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of zero point three. The covariance matrix is zero point three times the identity matrix. Despite this significant noise, the decoder maintains a token-level accuracy of over ninety-nine point nine percent. This combination of high fidelity and robustness provides a strong foundation for training Continuous Autoregressive Language Models.

The core of the CALM framework is an autoencoder that learns to map a group of K discrete tokens to a continuous vector and back. This mapping is bijective, meaning the encoder and decoder can perfectly reconstruct the original tokens from the vector. The encoder takes a sequence of K tokens and maps them to K embeddings. Each embedding is processed by a position-wise feed-forward network, producing K hidden states. These are flattened and compressed by a linear layer, reducing the dimension from Kd to d. This compressed representation is then passed through another feed-forward network and a linear projection to create the l-dimensional latent vector z. 

The decoder mirrors the encoder. It starts by transforming z with a linear layer and an FFN to get a d-dimensional hidden state. This is expanded by another linear layer to Kd dimensions and reshaped into K hidden states. Each of these is processed by a second FFN and projected to vocabulary logits using the same embedding matrix used for the encoder. The final step is to reconstruct the tokens by taking the argmax of these logits. 

The autoencoder is trained to minimize the reconstruction error using a cross-entropy loss across all K tokens. This loss is calculated from the logits produced by the decoder, not the reconstructed tokens. It is the negative sum of the log probabilities of each token given the latent vector derived from the encoder. 

Empirical tests show the architecture is effective and efficient. For example, when grouping four tokens, a latent vector of ten dimensions is enough for high-fidelity reconstruction. The autoencoder achieves over ninety-nine point nine percent accuracy at the token level with this setup. It’s also lightweight, using a shallow structure with a hidden dimension of five hundred and twelve. Its computational cost is nearly negligible compared to a language model.

The algorithm described in this section enables temperature sampling in CALM, a likelihood-free generative model. Unlike traditional methods that rescale logits, this approach uses rejection sampling to achieve the same goal. The method is exact and provably correct, relying on the principles of repeated sampling and probability exponentiation. 

The core idea starts with a simple case where the temperature is one divided by an integer. In this case, the target distribution is proportional to the original distribution raised to the power of that integer. The probability of drawing the same sample that many times in a row from the sampler is also proportional to this same value. This leads to a rejection sampling scheme where that many samples are drawn, and only if they are all identical are they accepted. Otherwise, the process restarts. This guarantees that the accepted samples follow the desired distribution.

For any temperature between zero and one, the algorithm breaks one over that temperature into an integer part and a fractional part. The first stage uses the repetition-based scheme for the integer part, producing a candidate sample only if that many independent draws are identical. The second stage deals with the fractional part. Here, the method uses the Bernoulli Factory theory to simulate a biased coin flip with a success probability of P(x) raised to the power of the fractional part. A sample is accepted only if it passes both stages. If it fails at any point, the process restarts.

The algorithm ensures that the generated samples follow P(x) raised to the power of one over the temperature, divided by a normalization constant. This is formally detailed in Algorithm 1, and the correctness is proven in Appendix A.1. The method provides a way to perform temperature sampling without needing access to the model's probability distribution, making it compatible with CALM's design.

The method starts by evaluating how well a model predicts the next token in a sequence, using a setup where the model is fed the correct previous tokens. To do this, two latent vectors are generated at each step. These vectors are then decoded using a frozen autoencoder's decoder, which means the decoder isn’t updated during this process. The Brier score, a metric for probabilistic predictions, is calculated using only the first token of each decoded chunk. However, this approach misses the quality of the remaining tokens in the sequence.  

To improve this, the authors introduce Brier-n, a new metric that evaluates the model’s performance on entire n-grams rather than just single tokens. In this method, each n-gram is treated as a single outcome. The Brier score is calculated for each n-gram, considering all tokens in the sequence together. This allows the evaluation to capture the quality of the entire sequence, not just the first token. The n-gram is treated as one unit, and the score reflects whether the model predicted the exact sequence of tokens in that chunk.  

The authors then combine the Brier-n scores for n equals one through four into a composite metric called BrierLM. This is done by taking the geometric mean of the four Brier-n scores. The geometric mean ensures that each n-gram’s contribution is balanced in the final score. To make the metric more interpretable, it is scaled by multiplying it by one hundred, placing it on a zero to one hundred range.  

The formula for BrierLM is one hundred multiplied by the product of the Brier-n scores for n equals one through four, raised to the power of one quarter. This formula ensures that the final score reflects the overall performance across different n-gram lengths. By using this approach, the evaluation becomes more comprehensive, capturing the model’s ability to predict not just single tokens but also sequences of tokens.

The exact algorithm struggles when the temperature is low. At these temperatures, the algorithm needs to draw n samples, where n is the floor of one divided by T. This leads to many rejected samples and poor use of the data. The problem is most serious when the temperature is very low. To fix this, an approximate algorithm is introduced for temperatures of the form T equals one divided by n. The idea is to move from a single, risky trial to a combinatorial search over a large batch of N samples, where N is much larger than n. This allows one batch to contain combinations of N choose n distinct candidates, improving sample use and increasing the chance of finding a match in one go. For example, when sampling at a temperature of one half, which means n equals two, a batch of ten samples might be drawn. In this example, sample A appears three times and sample B appears two times. The algorithm counts how many successful n-tuple candidates are in the batch. For sample A, there are three successful candidates, calculated as the combination of three choose two. For sample B, there is one successful candidate, calculated as the combination of two choose two. The output is then sampled from the set of valid candidates, which includes A and B, based on their weighted probabilities. In this example, the chance of picking A is three fourths, and the chance of picking B is one fourth. If no sample appears at least n times, the candidate set would be empty. To ensure the algorithm always gives an output, a fallback mechanism is added. This mechanism gradually lowers the matching requirement from n to n minus one, then n minus two, and so on, until a non-empty candidate set is found.

The algorithm is called Approximate Temperature Sampling. It takes a base sampler, a target temperature of one divided by n, and a batch size much larger than n. The output is a sample that follows a distribution proportional to the base sampler's distribution raised to the power of n.  

First, the algorithm draws a large batch of samples from the base sampler. Then it counts how many times each unique sample appears in the batch.  

Next, it starts with the value m equals n and works downwards. At each step, it creates a candidate set of samples that appear at least m times in the batch. Each candidate sample is given a weight based on the number of combinations possible from its count at that step.  

If a candidate set is successfully created, the algorithm stops checking lower steps. Once a valid candidate set is found, the algorithm selects a sample from it based on the weights assigned to each candidate. The selected sample is returned as the final output.  

The algorithm ensures a sample is always produced by gradually lowering the matching requirement from n to n minus one, then n minus two, and so on, until a non-empty candidate set is found.  

The weights are calculated using combinations. For each sample, the weight is the number of ways to choose m items from its count in the batch. This helps prioritize samples that appear more frequently.  

The algorithm is designed to approximate the target distribution efficiently. By using a large batch and adjusting the matching requirement, it balances accuracy and computational feasibility.

The algorithm has bias when using any finite batch size. This happens because the output probability depends on the ratio of weights calculated from a single stochastic batch. The expectation of a ratio isn’t usually the same as the ratio of expectations. This mismatch introduces bias into the results. However, the algorithm’s main advantage is that it becomes unbiased as the batch size grows infinitely large. When the batch size approaches infinity, the output distribution matches the true target distribution exactly. This is a key property, showing the algorithm’s reliability for large-scale use. The reason this works is that, with more data, the randomness averages out, and the approximation becomes exact. This important characteristic is stated formally in a theorem. The theorem confirms that the algorithm’s output distribution converges to the true distribution as the batch size increases without bound. This makes the method useful for applications where high accuracy is needed, provided enough data is available. The balance between bias and computational feasibility is handled by choosing an appropriate batch size.

Theorem 3 introduces two probability distributions. The first is P_alg, the chance of sampling x using Algorithm 2 with a batch size of N. The second is P_T, which equals P(x) raised to the power of n, divided by Z_T. Z_T is the sum of P(x) raised to the power of n for all possible x. The theorem says that as N grows very large, P_alg gets closer to P_T. This means the algorithm becomes unbiased in the limit of large batches. The proof for this is in Appendix A.3. This consistency makes the algorithm a principled way to approximate sampling. The batch size N acts like a control knob, letting users trade off between how fast the algorithm runs and how accurate it is. When N is large, accuracy improves but computation takes longer. When N is small, the method runs faster but introduces more bias. This gives practitioners flexibility. The theorem shows that with enough data, the method can match the true target distribution. It also explains why Algorithm 2 is reliable for sampling when resources allow for larger batches. The temperature is set to one divided by n, linking the algorithm’s behavior to the power n used in the distribution. This connection ensures the method aligns with the theoretical goals of sampling.

The algorithm uses a black-box sampling interface, which allows it to work with any implicit language model. This design means it is not limited to the CALM framework but can be used with all implicit language models. It serves as a universal toolkit for controlled decoding in discrete spaces. The approach avoids needing specific details about the model’s inner workings, making it adaptable. This universality comes from relying only on standard sampling methods. The method’s flexibility ensures it can be applied broadly across different models and tasks. Its design supports controlled generation without requiring model-specific adjustments.

The second is P_T(x), which equals P(x) raised to the power of n, divided by Z_T. Z_T is the sum of P(x) raised to the power of n for all possible x. The theorem says that as N grows larger, P_alg(x;N) gets closer to P_T(x). This means the algorithm becomes unbiased as the batch size increases. The batch size N acts as a practical lever to balance efficiency and accuracy. As N approaches infinity, the algorithm’s output matches the true target distribution. This makes the algorithm a principled approximation of the target distribution. The proof of this theorem is in Appendix A dot 3 of the paper. The theorem ensures that the method converges to the correct result as the batch size increases. The batch size N controls how closely the algorithm approximates the true distribution. Larger N means better accuracy but higher computational cost. This gives users a way to adjust the tradeoff between speed and precision. The theorem confirms that the method is consistent and reliable for practical use. The algorithm explicitly computes Z_T as the sum of P(x) raised to the power of n for all x. The algorithm is built to work with any black-box sampling interface. This means it doesn’t need to know the inner workings of the model it’s using. It just needs to call a sampling function. Because of this, the algorithm isn’t tied to the CALM framework. It can be used with any implicit language model. The design makes it flexible enough to apply to the whole class of such models. The algorithm isn’t limited to one specific setup. It acts as a universal toolkit. It helps with controlled decoding in discrete spaces. This makes it useful for a wide range of tasks. The approach avoids relying on model-specific details. Instead, it focuses on the interface. This allows it to work with any model that provides the right sampling function. The result is a method that’s easy to adapt and use across different systems.

The generative head is built from L residual MLP blocks. Each block takes the current noise representation and improves it step by step. The process starts with an initial noise vector called epsilon zero, which is the same as epsilon. 

Each block first combines the current noise representation with a hidden state. This is done using two linear layers. The result is passed through a SwiGLU layer, which has an intermediate dimension of d. This layer helps the model learn complex patterns in the data. 

After the SwiGLU layer, the block adds the original input back to the output. This is called a residual connection. It helps the model train more effectively by allowing gradients to flow through the network more easily. 

Once all L blocks have processed the noise, a final linear layer changes the representation to the target dimension l. This gives the final output vector, called Z sub i. 

The whole process is designed to take the initial noise and gradually transform it into a structured output. Using residual connections and SwiGLU layers allows the model to handle complex transformations while keeping training stable. The choice of L blocks and the intermediate dimension d controls how much the model can refine the noise before producing the final result.

narration: The Brier score is a theoretically sound measure, but it is difficult to calculate directly for CALM because it needs the full predictive distribution P. Instead, an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator can be made without using likelihoods, only using samples from the model. The uncertainty part of the Brier score, which is the sum of P(x) squared for all x, can be thought of as the chance that two independent samples from P are the same. An unbiased estimator for this uncertainty part is the indicator function that checks if two samples, one and two from P, are equal. The accuracy part of the Brier score, which is P(y), can be estimated using the indicator function that checks if a single sample from P equals y. By combining these two estimators, a practical and unbiased estimator for the Brier score can be created using two samples from the model. The formula for the estimator is the sum of two indicators checking if each sample equals y, minus an indicator checking if the two samples are equal. This estimator allows for evaluating CALM's predictive abilities without needing to calculate likelihoods. The method works by drawing two samples from the model's distribution, then comparing them to the target y and to each other. If the first sample matches y, that counts as one point. If the second sample matches y, that adds another point. But if the two samples are the same, that point is subtracted. This gives an estimate of the Brier score using only samples, without needing the full distribution. This approach is efficient and avoids the need for complex calculations involving probabilities.

The paper introduces two dropout methods to make the autoencoder's latent space more robust. The first applies dropout with a rate of fifteen percent to the latent vector before passing it to the decoder. This forces the model to learn a representation that can handle small errors from the downstream model. The second method randomly masks fifteen percent of the input tokens. This is similar to the CBOW method, where the model must infer the masked tokens from their context. This helps the latent vector capture the chunk's meaning, not just token indexes. Both methods are only used during training. They are turned off when training or using the language model later. 

For a chunk of four tokens, the latent vector has one hundred twenty-eight dimensions. This size allows the model to encode information redundantly. The encoder learns a posterior distribution where the standard deviations converge to approximately point three. When sampling the latent vector, this adds Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of point three times the identity matrix to the predicted mean. Despite this noise, the decoder still achieves more than ninety-nine point nine percent accuracy on tokens. This combination of high accuracy and robustness gives a strong base for training Continuous Autoregressive Language Models.

The original method evaluates next-token prediction by generating two latent vectors at each step, decoding them with a frozen autoencoder's decoder, and then computing the Brier score using only the first token of each chunk. This approach focuses solely on the first token, ignoring the quality of the rest of the sequence. To improve this, the authors introduce Brier-n, a new metric that evaluates the entire n-gram instead of just the first token.  

In Brier-n, the n-gram is treated as a single, atomic outcome. This means that instead of looking at individual tokens, the method considers the whole sequence of n tokens as one unit. The indicator functions in the Brier score are adjusted to reflect this change, allowing the metric to capture the quality of the entire n-gram.  

To create a more comprehensive evaluation, the authors combine Brier-n scores for n equals one through four into a single metric called BrierLM. This is done by taking the geometric mean of the four Brier-n scores. The geometric mean ensures that all n-gram lengths contribute equally to the final score.  

Finally, the BrierLM score is scaled by multiplying it by one hundred, placing it on a more interpretable zero to one hundred range. This makes it easier to understand and compare with other metrics. The formula for BrierLM is one hundred multiplied by the product of the Brier-n scores for n equals one through four, raised to the power of zero point two five. This approach provides a more complete picture of the model's performance by considering the quality of the entire sequence, not just the first token.

The model starts with discrete tokens as input instead of using latent vectors directly. This is because the Transformer struggles to understand meaning from compact latent representations. So during training, each step uses the previous K tokens as input. 

To keep things efficient, these K tokens are passed through a two-layer MLP. This compression module combines them into a single input representation. The MLP is lightweight, making the process fast and manageable.

During inference, the same idea applies. The previous K tokens are embedded and compressed using the same MLP. This compressed version becomes the input for the Transformer. The Transformer then outputs a hidden state, which is used to predict the next continuous vector. This vector is a smooth, dense representation of the next step.

But the process doesn’t stop there. The predicted continuous vector is passed through a frozen decoder. This decoder is part of a pre-trained autoencoder. It converts the continuous vector back into K discrete tokens. These tokens become the input for the next step, closing a feedback loop between the continuous and discrete representations.

This loop lets the model generate new tokens step by step, using both types of representations. The discrete tokens provide structure, while the continuous vectors allow for smooth transitions. The system is called CALM, and its design ensures that the model can efficiently handle both types of data. The whole process is illustrated in Figure 2.

To create the targets in the I-JEPA framework, start with an input image. This image is split into a sequence of non-overlapping patches. Each patch is a small part of the image, like a tile in a mosaic. These patches are then passed through a target-encoder, which is a neural network that transforms each patch into a representation. These representations are stored in a set called s-y. Each element in this set corresponds to one patch in the original image.  

Next, to get the targets for the loss function, randomly sample four blocks from the target representations. These blocks can be overlapping. Each block is represented by a mask called B-i. The patch-level representation of the i-th block is called s-y-i, which is a collection of the representations from the patches that fall within the mask B-i.  

When sampling the blocks, use a random aspect ratio between three quarters and one and a half. This means the blocks can be wider or taller but not too extreme. Also, use a random scale between one fifteenth and one fifth. This controls how large each block is relative to the original image.  

Importantly, the target blocks are obtained by masking the output of the target-encoder, not the input image. This ensures the target representations have a high semantic level. This distinction is crucial for the method to work effectively.  

Then, randomly sample a context block with a different scale range. Remove any overlapping target blocks from this context block. This step ensures the context block is informative yet sparse, making it efficient to process.

For every patch in the batch, you calculate the squared difference between each element of the predicted and target vectors. Then you sum those squared differences across all elements in the patch. You repeat this for every patch in the batch. Finally, you average all those patch contributions to get the total loss. This loss guides the model to minimize the difference between its predictions and the target representations. The algorithm is called Likelihood-free Temperature Sampling. It takes a base sampler for an implicit discrete distribution and a target temperature between zero and one. It returns a sample accepted with a probability proportional to the original distribution raised to the power of one divided by the temperature.  

The algorithm has two stages. The first handles the integer part of the reciprocal of the temperature. The second handles the fractional part.  

For the integer part, the algorithm draws a number of independent and identically distributed samples equal to the floor of the reciprocal of the temperature. If all the samples drawn are the same, that sample is chosen as the result of the first stage. If they are not all the same, the process restarts from the first stage.  

If the fractional part of the reciprocal of the temperature is zero, the result from the first stage is returned immediately.  

For the fractional part, the algorithm enters a loop. It draws a sample from the base sampler. If the sample matches the result from the first stage, that sample is returned immediately. If it does not match, a uniform random number between zero and one is drawn.  

If this number is less than the fractional part of the reciprocal of the temperature divided by the loop counter, the process restarts from the first stage. If it is not less than that value, the loop counter is incremented and the loop continues.  

This approach allows sampling at a given temperature without explicitly computing the likelihood. It uses repeated sampling and conditional checks to adjust the acceptance probability based on the temperature. The method ensures that the final sample is accepted with the correct probability, even when the original distribution is implicit.

The energy loss is a training objective built using the energy score, a scoring rule that measures how well predictions align with observations by comparing distances between samples. It doesn’t need probability densities, just samples. The energy score has two parts. The first part looks at the average distance between two samples from the predictive distribution. This part pushes the model to generate diverse outputs, avoiding cases where all samples are the same. The second part looks at the average distance between a sample and the ground truth. This part pushes the model to make predictions that are close to the actual observation.  

The expectations in the energy score can’t be calculated exactly, so we use a Monte Carlo estimator instead. This becomes the energy loss. To compute it, we draw eight candidate samples from the generative head at each step. These samples are generated by the model. We also draw one hundred target samples from the conditional Gaussian posterior, which is produced by the autoencoder. Using many target samples helps reduce the variance in the loss, making training more stable.  

The final energy loss combines the candidate and target samples. It calculates distances between all pairs of candidate samples, but only when the samples are different. It also calculates distances between each target and candidate. The loss is the sum of these distances, scaled by two divided by the product of the number of candidate and target samples for the target-candidate distances. For the candidate-candidate distances, the loss is scaled by one divided by the product of the number of candidates and one less than the number of candidates. This loss function encourages both diversity and accuracy in the model’s predictions. The small number of candidate samples keeps training efficient, while the large number of target samples helps keep the loss stable. The energy loss is flexible because it only needs the ability to generate samples, allowing the model to have a simple and efficient design.
