The goal here is to perform temperature sampling with a black-box sampler, which only generates samples without giving direct access to probabilities. The method works in two stages, using rejection sampling and ideas from probability exponentiation. 

Start by choosing a temperature between zero and one. Break one divided by the temperature into an integer part and a fractional part. The integer part is the floor of one divided by the temperature. The fractional part is one divided by the temperature minus the integer part. 

In the first stage, use the integer part. Draw that many samples from the black-box sampler. If all of them are identical, keep that sample. Otherwise, reject and try again. This ensures the distribution of accepted samples is proportional to the probability of x raised to the power of the integer part. 

Next, handle the fractional part. This requires a more complex step, inspired by the Bernoulli Factory theory. The idea is to simulate a biased coin flip with a success probability equal to the probability of x raised to the power of the fractional part. This is done iteratively, using the same black-box sampler. If the flip succeeds, keep the sample from the first stage. If not, reject and restart the whole process. 

The final distribution of accepted samples is proportional to the probability of x raised to the power of one divided by the temperature, divided by a normalization constant. This guarantees the exact temperature sampling without needing the model’s probabilities. 

The method is exact and provably correct, as shown in the theorem. The proof is in Appendix A.1. The next section discusses how many samples this method is expected to generate on average.

Posterior collapse happens in variational autoencoders when parts of the hidden space stop helping with reconstructing data. When this happens, those parts fully collapse to the standard normal prior, which is the default distribution used in VAEs. This collapse makes those dimensions uninformative for reconstruction. More importantly, they act like random noise, which can make training models that come after the VAE harder.  

To stop this from happening, the authors use a method called KL clipping. This method changes how the model is trained by limiting how low the KL divergence can go for each part of the hidden space. The KL divergence measures how much the model’s learned distribution differs from the standard normal prior.  

For each part of the hidden space, the KL divergence is compared to a minimum value. If the KL divergence drops below that minimum, the minimum value is used instead. This minimum value is called lambda KL, and the authors set it to half.  

This method ensures that each part of the hidden space contributes to reconstructing the input data. By keeping the KL divergence from going too low, the model is encouraged to use all parts of the hidden space actively. This prevents parts from collapsing and helps create a more organized and useful representation of the data.  

The reason this works is because it stops dimensions from becoming pure noise. These noise dimensions would otherwise introduce a chaotic signal that interferes with the training of the downstream language model. By keeping all dimensions active, the model learns a structured and meaningful representation of the data.

The paper introduces variational regularization to build a smoother latent space. Instead of mapping inputs directly to a fixed latent vector, the encoder now outputs two vectors: mu and sigma. These define a diagonal Gaussian distribution from which the latent vector is sampled. The sampling happens by drawing from a normal distribution with mean mu and variance sigma squared times the identity matrix. This change adds randomness to the encoding process.  

A new term is added to the loss function: the KL divergence loss. This measures how much the encoded distribution differs from a standard normal prior with zero mean and identity covariance. The total loss becomes a weighted sum of the reconstruction loss and the KL divergence loss. A hyperparameter called beta controls how much weight to give to the regularization term. The paper sets beta to a small value, like one thousandth, to keep the regularization gentle.  

The KL divergence is calculated using a specific formula. It involves summing terms that include the log of sigma squared, sigma squared itself, and mu squared. Each of these terms is multiplied by negative one-half. This formula ensures that the encoded distribution stays close to the standard normal prior.  

This approach prevents the encoder from using overly precise or large values in the latent space. By encouraging the latent vectors to stay near the origin, the method promotes a smoother and more structured latent manifold. This makes the space better suited for tasks like generative modeling, where smoothness helps in creating realistic outputs.

The energy loss is a training objective built using the energy score, a scoring rule that compares predictions to observations without needing probability densities. It measures alignment by looking at distances between samples instead of densities. For a predictive distribution P and a ground truth observation y, the energy score is the expected distance between two samples from P, minus twice the expected distance between a sample from P and y. This score is strictly proper for any value between zero and two, and that value is usually set to one.  

The first part of the energy score encourages diversity by penalizing predictions that are too similar or overly confident. The second part pushes predictions closer to the ground truth, improving fidelity. Calculating the energy score exactly is not possible, so we use an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator as the energy loss.  

To compute this, we draw eight candidate samples from the generative head at each step. The autoencoder maps a token chunk to a conditional Gaussian posterior instead of a fixed point. Using a single sample as ground truth can add too much variance, so we draw one hundred target samples from the posterior to stabilize training.  

The final energy loss combines distances between target samples and candidate samples, and between candidate samples themselves. When calculating distances between candidate samples, we only consider distinct pairs, not including when a sample is compared to itself. This helps avoid overcounting.  

The exponent used in the distance calculation is typically one, but it can vary between zero and two. This value affects how the model weighs diversity and fidelity.  

We use eight model samples to keep training efficient, as each sample requires evaluating the generative head. Drawing one hundred target samples from a known Gaussian posterior has minimal overhead, which helps reduce loss variance.  

This likelihood-free approach only needs the ability to draw samples from the generative head. It allows flexible designs with few constraints on the internal architecture, making it simple and efficient.

The modified context block is then passed through the context encoder, which is called f theta. This encoder produces a patch-level representation of the context block. The context encoder plays a key role in transforming the visual information into a structured format. This structured format helps the model understand the spatial relationships within the image. The output of the encoder is used later in the process to predict the target blocks. 

This setup ensures that the model learns to extract meaningful features from the context block while ignoring redundant information. The result is a more focused and effective learning process.

The method described here is for exact temperature sampling in the CALM framework, where the generative head is a black-box sampler with no access to the probability distribution. The goal is to adjust the sampling temperature without needing explicit probabilities. 

The algorithm is based on rejection sampling. For a temperature value of one divided by an integer, the target distribution is proportional to the original distribution raised to the power of that integer. To achieve this, the algorithm draws that many samples and only accepts them if all of them are identical. This ensures the accepted samples follow the desired distribution. 

For any temperature between zero and one, the exponent one divided by the temperature is split into an integer part and a fractional part. The integer part is handled using the repetition-based scheme described earlier. The fractional part requires a more complex approach inspired by the Bernoulli Factory theory. This involves simulating a biased coin flip where the success probability is the original distribution raised to the power of the fractional part. 

A sample is accepted only if it passes both stages of the algorithm. If it fails at any stage, the entire process restarts. This ensures the generated samples follow the temperature-adjusted distribution. 

The algorithm is formally detailed in Algorithm 1. The correctness of the method is guaranteed by Theorem 1, which states that the generated samples follow the specified distribution formula. The proof of this theorem is provided in Appendix A.1. 

This approach allows temperature sampling in CALM without needing explicit access to the probability distribution. It ensures the generated samples follow the desired temperature-adjusted distribution. The next section likely discusses the computational efficiency of this method.

The paper introduces two dropout methods to improve the robustness of the autoencoder's latent space. The first applies a dropout rate of fifteen percent to the latent vector before it goes to the decoder. This forces the model to learn a representation that can handle small errors from the generative model downstream. The second method masks fifteen percent of input tokens during training. This is similar to how the Continuous Bag-of-Words method works, where the model predicts masked tokens from their context. This helps the latent vector capture semantic meaning instead of just token indexes. Both dropout techniques are used only during the autoencoder's training. They are turned off when training or using the continuous language model. 

The autoencoder processes chunks of four tokens and uses a latent vector with one hundred twenty-eight dimensions. This gives it enough space to encode information redundantly. The encoder learns a posterior distribution where the standard deviations settle around point three. When sampling the latent vector, this adds a Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of point three along each dimension, like an identity matrix. Despite this noise, the decoder still manages to predict tokens with over ninety-nine point nine percent accuracy. The resulting vector representation is both accurate and robust, making it a strong base for training Continuous Autoregressive Language Models.

The model starts with discrete tokens instead of latent vectors. The first idea was to take the previous latent vectors and project them into the Transformer's hidden space using a linear layer. But this didn't work well. The model had trouble understanding the meaning from those compact vectors, which made performance drop. 

So the team switched to using discrete tokens from the previous step as input. During training, each step uses K tokens from the step before. To keep things efficient, they added a two-layer MLP. This module takes the K token embeddings and combines them into a single input representation. 

At inference time, the last K tokens are embedded and run through the same MLP to create a single input. This goes into the Transformer. The Transformer then produces a hidden state. This hidden state is used by an energy-based head to predict the next continuous vector. 

Once the continuous vector is predicted, it's passed through the frozen decoder of a pre-trained autoencoder. This decoder turns the vector back into the next K discrete tokens. This creates a loop between continuous and discrete representations. 

The whole system is called CALM. The input process uses discrete tokens to help the model understand better. The MLP keeps things efficient by reducing K tokens to one input. The energy-based head and autoencoder decoder handle the transition between continuous and discrete spaces. This setup allows the model to generate new tokens step by step while keeping the input manageable.

The CALM framework starts with an autoencoder that learns to map K discrete tokens to a continuous vector and back. This autoencoder has two parts: an encoder that turns token sequences into vectors and a decoder that rebuilds token sequences from vectors. The encoder works on each chunk of K tokens without considering the rest of the sequence. That makes it context-free, which keeps things simple and fast. A version that uses context from earlier tokens is something to explore later.

The encoder first turns each of the K tokens into an embedding. Then, each embedding goes through a position-wise feed-forward network. These K hidden states are flattened and squeezed down with a linear layer, reducing the dimension from Kd to d. This compressed version moves through another feed-forward network and a linear layer to create the l-dimensional latent vector z.

The decoder starts with z, passing it through a linear layer and a feed-forward network to get a d-dimensional hidden state. This state is then expanded with another linear layer to Kd dimensions and reshaped into K hidden states. Each of these goes through a feed-forward network again and is projected to vocabulary logits using the same embedding matrix the encoder used. Finally, the tokens are chosen by picking the highest logit for each position.

The autoencoder is trained to minimize the reconstruction error using cross-entropy loss across all K tokens. This means it tries to make the probability of each token in the original sequence as high as possible, given the latent vector from the encoder.

With K set to four tokens and a latent vector of ten dimensions, the model achieves over ninety-nine point nine percent accuracy on each token. The encoder and decoder are lightweight, with a hidden dimension of five hundred twelve, making them much faster than typical language models.

The prediction process starts with the output of the context encoder, called s x. This is used to predict m target block representations, labeled s y one through s y m. For each target block s y i, the predictor g phi takes two inputs: the context encoder output s x and a set of mask tokens for each patch that needs to be predicted.  

Each mask token is linked to a specific target mask b i, which defines the patches that need to be predicted for that target block. The mask tokens are created using a shared learnable vector. This vector is modified by adding a positional embedding to account for the position of each patch.  

The predictor g phi processes the context encoder output and the mask tokens for each target block. It outputs a prediction for each patch in the target block, resulting in a set of predicted values labeled as hat s y i. Each prediction in hat s y i is a set of predicted patch level representations, labeled as hat s y j for each patch j in the target block.  

This process is repeated m times, once for each target block. Each iteration uses the mask tokens corresponding to the patches in that target block. As a result, we get m sets of predicted values, hat s y one through hat s y m, each corresponding to a different target block.  

The reason for using mask tokens is to guide the predictor to focus on specific patches that need to be predicted. The shared learnable vector allows the model to adapt the mask tokens across different patches, while the positional embedding ensures the model understands the spatial arrangement of the patches. This helps the predictor generate accurate predictions for each target block.

The Brier score is a theoretically sound measure, but calculating it directly for CALM is not possible because it requires knowing the full predictive distribution P. Instead, we can create an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator for the Brier score without using likelihoods, by using only samples from the model.  

The uncertainty part of the Brier score, which is the sum of P(x) squared over all x, can be thought of as the probability that two independent samples from P are the same. An unbiased estimator for this uncertainty term is an indicator function that checks if two samples, one called sample one and another called sample two, drawn from P, are equal.  

The accuracy part of the Brier score, which is P(y), can be estimated using a single sample from P by checking if that sample equals y. This means we take one sample and compare it directly to the target y.  

By combining these estimators, a practical and unbiased estimator for the Brier score can be created using two samples from P. The formula for this estimator is the sum of two indicator functions checking if each sample equals y, minus an indicator function checking if the two samples are equal.  

This estimator allows for evaluating CALM's predictive abilities without needing to calculate the full likelihood. It uses just two samples from the model and compares them to the target in a simple way.

The method starts by evaluating how well a model predicts the next token in a sequence, using a teacher-forcing setup. At each step, two latent vectors are generated and decoded using a frozen autoencoder’s decoder. The Brier score is then calculated, but only for the first token of each chunk. This gives a basic measure of performance, but it misses the quality of the rest of the generated tokens.  

To improve this, the authors introduce Brier-n, a new way to compute the Brier score over entire n-grams. Instead of looking at each token separately, Brier-n treats each n-gram as a single outcome. This means the indicator functions in the estimator consider the whole sequence of tokens together, not individually. This change better captures the overall quality of the generated text.  

The next step is to combine the Brier-n scores for different values of n. The authors use a composite metric called BrierLM, which is the geometric mean of the Brier-n scores for n equals one through four. This approach follows the same logic as metrics like BLEU, which also use multiple n-gram values to evaluate language quality.  

To make the metric more interpretable, the final BrierLM score is scaled by multiplying it by one hundred. This puts the score on a zero to one hundred range, making it easier to understand and compare across different models. The formula for BrierLM is one hundred multiplied by the product of the Brier-n scores for n equals one through four, all raised to the power of one quarter. This ensures that each Brier-n score contributes equally to the final result.

Each block in the stack takes the current version of the noise vector and combines it with a hidden state. This is done using two linear layers, which transform the data step by step. After this combination, a SwiGLU layer is applied. This layer has an intermediate dimension of d, which controls how much the data is expanded before being compressed again. 

Then, a residual connection adds the original input of the block back to its output. This helps the model learn better by keeping some of the original information. 

After all L blocks have processed the data, a final linear layer is used. This layer changes the size of the representation from whatever it was to the target dimension l. The result is the output vector Z sub i. 

This design allows the model to refine the initial noise in a step-by-step way, using both the hidden state and residual connections to guide the process. The SwiGLU layer adds non-linearity and flexibility, while the residual connections help the model retain important features from earlier steps. The final linear layer ensures the output has the right size for whatever task it’s used for.

The core of the CALM framework is an autoencoder that learns to map a group of K discrete tokens to a continuous vector and back. This autoencoder has two main parts: an encoder and a decoder. The encoder takes a sequence of K tokens and turns them into a continuous vector. The decoder does the reverse, turning that vector back into the original token sequence. 

The encoder starts by converting each token in the input sequence into an embedding. Each of these embeddings is then passed through a position-wise feed-forward network. This gives K hidden states, which are then flattened and compressed by a linear layer that reduces the dimension from Kd to d. This compressed representation is then passed through another feed-forward network and a linear projection to create the l-dimensional latent vector z. 

The decoder mirrors the encoder. It starts by transforming the latent vector z using a linear layer and an FFN to get a d-dimensional hidden state. This hidden state is then expanded by a linear layer to a Kd-dimensional vector and reshaped into a sequence of K hidden states. Each of these states is passed through another FFN and then projected to vocabulary logits using the same embedding matrix used for the encoder. The tokens are then reconstructed by taking the argmax of these logits, selecting the most probable token at each position.

The autoencoder is trained to minimize the reconstruction error using a cross-entropy loss across all K token positions. This means the model learns to predict each token in the original sequence based on the latent vector. 

This design is efficient and effective. For example, when grouping four tokens, a latent vector with ten dimensions achieves over ninety-nine point nine percent accuracy in reconstructing tokens. The autoencoder has a shallow architecture and a hidden dimension of five hundred and twelve, making it lightweight and computationally efficient. It processes each token chunk independently, without relying on surrounding context.

The algorithm is called Likelihood-free Temperature Sampling. It samples from a distribution with a given temperature. It takes a base sampler for an implicit discrete distribution and a target temperature between zero and one. The output is a sample accepted with a probability proportional to the original distribution raised to the power of one divided by the temperature.  

The first step is to calculate an integer part of the reciprocal of the temperature, called n. Then calculate a fractional part of the reciprocal of the temperature, called alpha.  

In the first stage, the algorithm draws n independent and identically distributed samples from the base sampler. If all of these samples are the same, the algorithm keeps that sample as the current best. If they are not all the same, the algorithm restarts the first stage.  

If the fractional part alpha is zero, the algorithm returns the current best sample.  

In the second stage, the algorithm enters a loop where it draws a new sample from the base sampler. If the new sample is the same as the current best, the algorithm returns the current best. If the new sample is different, the algorithm draws a uniform random number between zero and one.  

If this number is less than alpha divided by the loop counter, the algorithm restarts the first stage. Otherwise, the algorithm increments the loop counter and continues the loop.  

This approach allows sampling from a distribution adjusted by temperature without explicitly computing the likelihood. The integer part ensures multiple samples are drawn and checked for consistency, while the fractional part introduces a controlled chance to restart based on the loop counter. This balances exploration and consistency in the sampled output.

The energy loss is a training objective built using the energy score, a scoring rule that works without needing probability densities. It measures how well predictions align with observations by looking at distances between samples. For a predictive distribution P and a ground truth observation y, the energy score is the average distance between two samples from P, minus twice the average distance between a sample from P and y. This score works well for any alpha between zero and two, and alpha is usually set to one.  

The first part of the energy score pushes the model to be diverse, avoiding situations where all generated samples are the same. The second part makes the model predictions stay close to the actual observation, ensuring accuracy.  

Because the energy score uses averages that are hard to compute exactly, we use a Monte Carlo method instead. This means we draw eight candidate samples from the generative head at each step. To reduce variance, we also draw one hundred target samples from a conditional Gaussian posterior instead of relying on a single ground-truth sample. This posterior is defined as q(⋅|x_{(i−1)K+1:iK}), a distribution conditioned on the input token chunk.  

The final energy loss combines these samples. It calculates the average distance between target samples and candidate samples, then subtracts the average distance between the candidate samples themselves. The distance used is the Euclidean distance raised to the power of alpha, which is typically one.  

Drawing one hundred target samples from a known Gaussian posterior has almost no extra cost, so using a large M is possible. The energy loss is flexible because it only needs the ability to generate samples, not complex probability calculations. This lets the model’s internal design stay simple and efficient.

narration: The loss measures how well the model predicts patch-level representations by comparing them to target representations. It is calculated as the average distance between predicted and target patch-level representations. The formula sums the distances between predicted and target representations for all patches. Each patch's distance is calculated by summing the squared differences between predicted and target representations for all elements in the patch's batch. The loss is the average of all these distances across the entire batch. The parameters of the predictor and context encoder are learned using gradient-based optimization. The target encoder's parameters are updated using an exponential moving average of the context-encoder parameters. Using an exponential moving average for the target encoder is important for training JEAs with Vision Transformers. The same approach of using an exponential moving average for the target encoder is found to be important for I-JEPA. The exponential moving average helps stabilize training by ensuring the target encoder doesn't change too rapidly. This allows the model to learn more effectively from the target representations. The moving average is computed by taking a weighted average of the current context encoder parameters and the previous target encoder parameters. The weight is typically a small value, like fifteen percent, which controls how much the target encoder updates with each step. This ensures the target encoder remains consistent while still adapting to new information.

narration:
Posterior collapse happens when some latent dimensions in a variational autoencoder stop helping with reconstruction and act like random noise instead. When this happens, the KL divergence for those dimensions drops to zero, making them useless for learning. Worse, these noise-like dimensions create a chaotic signal that messes up the training of the downstream language model, making it unstable. 

To fix this, the authors use a method called KL clipping. This changes the training objective by setting a minimum value for the KL divergence loss of each dimension. The minimum value is called lambda KL, and they set it to half. This means that even if a dimension’s KL divergence would normally be lower than half, it gets counted as half instead. 

By doing this, every dimension is forced to contribute to the reconstruction of the input. This stops the posterior collapse and helps the model learn a dense, structured representation of the data. The method ensures that no dimension is left out, keeping the learning process stable and effective. 

The paper explains that this problem showed up in their model as some latent dimensions completely collapsing to the standard normal prior. This collapse made those dimensions useless for reconstruction and introduced noise that disrupted training. The solution of KL clipping prevents this by keeping each dimension’s contribution above a certain threshold, ensuring they all play a role in the model’s learning.

The paper introduces two dropout techniques to improve the robustness of an autoencoder's latent space. The first applies a dropout rate of fifteen percent to the latent vector z before it goes to the decoder. This forces the model to learn a representation that can handle small errors from the generative model downstream. The second method randomly masks fifteen percent of input tokens during training. This is similar to the CBOW approach, where the model learns to infer masked tokens from their context. Instead of just compressing token indexes, this enriches the latent vector with semantic meaning from the surrounding tokens. Both dropout methods are only used during the autoencoder's training phase and are turned off when training or using the continuous language model. 

For a chunk of four tokens, the autoencoder uses a latent vector with one hundred twenty-eight dimensions. This gives the model enough capacity to encode information redundantly. The encoder learns a posterior distribution where the standard deviations converge to approximately point three. When sampling the latent vector z, this adds a significant amount of Gaussian noise, roughly point three times the identity matrix, to the predicted mean. Despite this large perturbation, the decoder still manages to achieve a token-level accuracy of over ninety-nine point nine percent. The resulting vector representation is both accurate and robust, making it a strong foundation for Continuous Autoregressive Language Models.

The method is called variational regularization, and it changes a standard autoencoder into a variational one to create a smoother latent space. Instead of directly mapping an input to a single vector z, the encoder now outputs two vectors: mu and sigma. These define a diagonal Gaussian distribution from which the latent vector z is sampled. This introduces randomness into the encoding process.  

A new term is added to the total loss function called the KL divergence loss. It measures how much the encoded distribution differs from a standard normal prior, which has zero mean and identity covariance. This loss encourages the encoder to produce latent vectors that are close to this standard normal distribution.  

The total loss is a weighted sum of the reconstruction loss and the KL divergence loss. The weight is controlled by a hyperparameter called beta, which is set to one thousandth. This value balances how much emphasis is placed on regularization versus reconstruction.  

The KL divergence loss is calculated using a formula that involves the sum of terms related to sigma squared and mu squared. Each term includes the logarithm of sigma squared, as well as the negative of sigma squared and mu squared. The entire sum is multiplied by negative one half. This formula ensures the encoder avoids using very large or very precise values in z.  

By doing this, the latent space becomes more regularized and structured. This helps generative models work better because the latent manifold is smoother and more predictable.

To create the targets in the I-JEPA framework, start with an input image. This image is split into a sequence of non-overlapping patches. Each patch is a small part of the image, like a puzzle piece. These patches are then passed through a target-encoder, which turns each patch into a representation. All these representations are stored in a set called s-y. Each element in s-y represents one patch in the image. 

Next, randomly sample M blocks from these representations. The number of blocks, M, is usually set to four. These blocks can overlap, meaning a single patch can be part of more than one block. For each block, create a mask called B-i. This mask shows which patches are included in the block. The representation of the i-th block is called s-y-i, and it includes the patch-level representations of the patches in the block. 

When sampling these blocks, use a random aspect ratio between three quarters and one and a half. This means the blocks can be taller or wider but not too extreme. Also, use a random scale between fifteen percent and twenty percent. This scale controls the size of the blocks relative to the image. Importantly, the blocks are sampled from the output of the target-encoder, not the original image. This ensures the target representations have a high semantic level. 

After sampling the target blocks, randomly sample a context block with a scale between eighty-five percent and one hundred percent. This context block is larger and covers more of the image. Remove any overlapping target blocks from this context block. This makes the context block informative but sparse, which is efficient to process. The target blocks are relatively semantic, making them useful for the loss function.

The prediction process starts with the output of the context encoder, called s x. This output is used to predict M different target block representations, labeled s y one through s y M. For each of these target blocks, the predictor, called g phi, takes two inputs. The first is the context encoder output, s x, and the second is a set of mask tokens. These mask tokens are specific to the patches that need to be predicted for that target block. 

Each mask token is linked to a target mask, labeled B i, which tells us exactly which patches are to be predicted for the current target block. The mask tokens themselves come from a shared learnable vector. This means all mask tokens are generated from the same base vector, but each one gets a positional embedding added to it. These positional embeddings give information about where each patch is located in the image or sequence.

The predictor g phi takes the context encoder output and the mask tokens for a specific target block and produces a prediction for each patch in that block. This prediction is a set of values, labeled hat s y i, where each value corresponds to a specific patch in the target block. Each of these predicted values is labeled as hat s y j for patch j.

Since there are M target blocks, the predictor is applied M times. Each time, it uses mask tokens that match the positions of the patches being predicted for that particular target block. This results in M sets of predicted values, each set corresponding to one of the M target blocks.

The model starts with discrete tokens as input, avoiding the use of latent vectors that caused performance issues. Instead of projecting latent vectors into the Transformer's hidden space, it uses K tokens from the previous step. These tokens are embedded and compressed into a single input representation using a two-layer MLP. This compression module keeps things efficient while preserving needed information.  

During training, each step's input is built from the K tokens generated in the previous step. The compression module takes those K embeddings and maps them into one compact representation. This is then fed into the Transformer.  

At inference, step i begins with the previously generated K tokens. These are embedded and compressed the same way as during training. The resulting input representation is passed into the Transformer, which outputs a hidden state. This hidden state is used by an energy-based generative head to predict the next continuous vector.  

Once the continuous vector is predicted, it goes through a frozen decoder from a pre-trained autoencoder. This decoder reconstructs the next K discrete tokens. This creates a feedback loop, connecting continuous predictions back to discrete tokens.  

The process ensures that the model stays grounded in the discrete token space while still making continuous predictions. The use of a frozen decoder keeps the autoencoder's parameters fixed, avoiding unnecessary updates. The two-layer MLP in the compression module is lightweight, keeping the overall architecture efficient. The feedback loop helps maintain consistency between the continuous and discrete parts of the model. The full architecture, called CALM, is shown in Figure 2.

narration: The Brier score is a theoretically sound measure, but calculating it directly for CALM is not possible because it needs the full predictive distribution P. Instead, an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator can be created without using likelihoods, by only using samples from the model. The uncertainty part of the Brier score, which is the sum of P(x) squared over all x, can be thought of as the chance that two independent samples from P are the same. An unbiased estimator for this uncertainty part is an indicator function that checks if two samples, one and two from P, are equal. The accuracy part of the Brier score, which is P(y), can be estimated using a single sample from P by checking if that sample equals y. By combining these estimators, a practical and unbiased estimator for the Brier score is created using two samples from P. This estimator is given by the sum of two indicator functions checking if each sample equals y, minus an indicator function checking if the two samples are equal. This estimator allows for evaluating CALM's predictive abilities without needing to calculate likelihoods. The method relies on generating two independent samples from the model's distribution. For each sample, check if it matches the true outcome y. Then check if the two samples match each other. Add the two matches with y and subtract the match between the samples. This gives an estimate of the Brier score. The approach avoids complex calculations by using simple comparisons between samples. It works because the Brier score can be broken into parts that are easy to estimate with random samples.

narration:
The core of the CALM framework is an autoencoder that learns to map a group of K discrete tokens to a continuous vector and back. This mapping is bijective, meaning it can reconstruct the original tokens from the vector. The encoder takes a sequence of K tokens and maps them to K embeddings, each processed by a position-wise feed-forward network. These K hidden states are then flattened and compressed by a linear layer that reduces the dimension from Kd to d. This compressed representation is passed through another feed-forward network and a linear projection to produce an l-dimensional latent vector z. 

The decoder mirrors the encoder’s structure. It starts by transforming z using a linear layer and a feed-forward network to get a d-dimensional hidden state. This state is then expanded by a linear layer to Kd dimensions and reshaped into a sequence of K hidden states. Each of these is processed by another feed-forward network and projected to vocabulary logits using the same embedding matrix used in the encoder. Tokens are reconstructed by taking the argmax of these logits. 

The autoencoder is trained to minimize the reconstruction error using cross-entropy loss across all K tokens. This loss is the negative sum of the log probabilities of each token given the latent vector derived from the encoder. The model is lightweight, with a shallow architecture and a hidden dimension of five hundred twelve. When grouping four tokens, a latent vector of ten dimensions achieves over ninety-nine point nine percent accuracy in reconstructing tokens. This efficiency makes the autoencoder highly effective for the task.

narration: Posterior collapse happens in variational autoencoders when some parts of the hidden representation stop carrying useful information and instead act like random noise. This makes those parts unhelpful for reconstructing the input data. When a dimension collapses, its KL divergence drops to zero, which means it no longer contributes anything meaningful to the reconstruction. This is a problem because these noise-like parts create unpredictable signals that make training downstream models harder. The signals they produce are chaotic and can mess up the learning process. To fix this, the authors use a method called KL clipping. This method changes how the model is trained by setting a minimum value for each dimension’s KL loss. The KL divergence measures how much the hidden representation differs from a standard normal distribution. With KL clipping, the model ensures that each part of the hidden representation contributes meaningfully to reconstruction. The minimum value they use is called lambda KL, and they set it to one half. This technique stops the latent dimensions from collapsing completely and instead keeps them active and useful. By doing this, the model avoids posterior collapse and creates a more structured and dense hidden representation. The latent dimensions are kept from fully collapsing to the standard normal prior, ensuring they remain informative for reconstruction.

narration:
The loss measures how far the predicted patch representations are from the target ones. It uses the square of the difference between each pair of representations. For each patch, you calculate this distance and then average them across all patches. The loss is the average of these squared differences. 

Each patch has a predicted representation and a target representation. The distance between them is the sum of the squared differences of each element in the vectors. You do this for every element in the patch’s representation. Then you add up all these squared differences for every patch and divide by the total number of patches. This gives you the loss value. 

The predictor and context encoder parameters are learned by optimizing this loss using gradient descent. The target encoder parameters are updated using an exponential moving average of the context encoder’s parameters. This means the target encoder doesn’t change rapidly but instead follows the context encoder’s updates smoothly. 

This approach is important for training models like Vision Transformers. The exponential moving average helps stabilize the learning process. It ensures the target encoder stays aligned with the context encoder without changing too quickly. The same method works well for I-JEPA, showing its effectiveness across different models. 

The loss is a simple measure of how well the model predicts the target representations. It directly guides the training process by telling the model how to adjust its parameters to reduce the distance between predicted and target representations.

narration:
The CALM framework doesn’t give direct access to the probability distribution. It only gives a sampler. So we need a way to do temperature sampling without knowing the actual probabilities. The solution is a rejection sampling method that works with just the sampler.  

The idea comes from how repeating samples affects probabilities. If you want a temperature of one divided by an integer n, the target distribution is proportional to P(x) raised to the power of n. The chance of getting the same sample n times in a row from the sampler is exactly P(x) to the power of n. So the algorithm draws n samples and only accepts them if they are all the same. If not, it starts over. This gives the right distribution for that temperature.  

For any temperature T between zero and one, we split one divided by T into an integer part n and a fractional part alpha. The first stage uses the repetition method for the integer part. It draws n samples and only keeps them if they are all identical. The second stage handles the fractional part alpha. This needs a way to simulate a biased coin flip with a success probability of P(x) to the power of alpha. This is done using the Bernoulli Factory method.  

A sample must pass both stages to be accepted. If it fails at any stage, the entire process restarts. This ensures the final distribution is exactly proportional to P(x) raised to the power of one divided by T, divided by a normalization constant. The method is exact and proven correct. The full steps are in Algorithm 1.  

The key is that this works with only a sampler, not the full probability distribution. It avoids needing to calculate or access the distribution directly. This makes it compatible with the CALM framework.

narration: The paper introduces Brier-n, a way to extend the Brier score to evaluate language models using n-grams. The first step is to look at next-token prediction in a teacher-forcing setup. Here, two latent vectors are generated at each step. These vectors are decoded using a frozen autoencoder’s decoder. Then, the Brier score is calculated using only the first token from each chunk. But this method misses the quality of the rest of the tokens after the first one. To fix this, Brier-n considers the whole n-gram as a single outcome. This means the indicator functions treat the n-gram as one unit instead of separate tokens. The final metric, called BrierLM, combines Brier-n scores for n from one to four. It takes the geometric mean of these scores, which involves multiplying them together and then taking the one-quarter power of the product. This is done to follow the same pattern as metrics like BLEU. After that, the result is scaled by one hundred to make it easier to interpret, placing it on a zero to one hundred range. This approach ensures that the evaluation considers not just single tokens but also how well the model predicts sequences of tokens, making it more comprehensive.

The model starts with a discrete token input to handle its autoregressive process. Instead of using compact latent vectors directly, it uses K tokens from the previous step as input. This helps the model better understand the context and meaning in the data.  

To keep things efficient, a two-layer MLP is used to compress the K token embeddings into a single input representation. This compressed input is then fed into the Transformer. The MLP acts as a lightweight compression module, making sure the input is manageable for the Transformer to process.  

During inference, at each step, the model takes the previously generated K tokens. These tokens are first embedded and then compressed using the same MLP. The compressed result becomes the input to the Transformer. The Transformer processes this input and outputs a hidden state.  

This hidden state is then used by an energy-based generative head to predict the next continuous vector. This vector is a prediction of the next step in the sequence. Once predicted, the vector is passed through a frozen decoder of a pre-trained autoencoder. This decoder reconstructs the next K discrete tokens, closing the feedback loop.  

The process ensures that the model can generate new tokens step by step, using both the continuous and discrete representations. The use of a pre-trained autoencoder’s decoder helps maintain consistency with the discrete token space, ensuring the model stays grounded in meaningful representations.  

This setup allows the model to efficiently handle the input while maintaining the ability to generate accurate and meaningful outputs. The discrete token input is a key part of the CALM architecture, enabling the model to work with both continuous and discrete representations seamlessly.

The targets in I-JEPA are built from image blocks. Start with an image, split it into non-overlapping patches. Each patch is a small part of the image, like a puzzle piece. Feed all these patches into the target-encoder, which turns each one into a representation. These representations are stored in a set called s-y. Each entry in s-y is the representation of a single patch. 

To create the targets for the loss function, randomly pick M blocks from the set of representations. M is usually four. These blocks can overlap. For each block, create a mask called B-i. This mask tells which patches are included in the block. The representation of the i-th block is made by collecting all the patch representations that fall inside B-i. 

The blocks are sampled with a random aspect ratio between three quarters and one and a half. This means the block can be taller than it is wide or wider than it is tall. The scale of each block is between fifteen percent and twenty percent. This makes the blocks small compared to the whole image. 

Importantly, the blocks are sampled from the output of the target-encoder, not the original image. This ensures the target representations are high-level and semantic. 

In examples, four target blocks are chosen with the same scale and aspect ratio ranges. Then, a context block is sampled with a scale between eighty five percent and one hundred percent. Any target blocks that overlap with the context block are removed. This keeps the context block informative but sparse, making it efficient to process. The target blocks remain semantic while the context block stays sparse.

narration: The Brier score is a theoretically sound measure, but it is difficult to calculate directly for CALM because it needs the full predictive distribution P. Instead, we build an unbiased estimator using only samples from P, without needing likelihoods. The uncertainty part of the Brier score is the sum of P(x) squared over all x. This equals the probability that two independent samples from P are the same. To estimate this, take two samples from P and check if they are equal. If they are, the indicator is one, otherwise zero. For the accuracy part, which is P(y), take one sample from P and check if it equals y. If it does, the indicator is one, otherwise zero. To combine these, take two samples from P. Check if the first equals y, and if the second equals y. Add those two indicators together. Then subtract an indicator that checks if the two samples are equal. This gives the Brier score estimator. It uses two samples from P and calculates the sum of two indicators for whether each sample equals y, minus an indicator for whether the two samples are the same. This estimator allows evaluating CALM’s predictive abilities without needing to calculate likelihoods. The approach avoids complex computations by relying on simple comparisons between samples. It works because the estimator is unbiased and only requires sampling from the model.

narration:
The energy loss is a training objective built using the energy score, a scoring rule that does not require probability density evaluations. It measures how well predictions align with observations by comparing distances between samples.  

The energy score compares two things: the distance between two samples from a predictive distribution and the distance between a sample from that distribution and the ground truth observation. This score works well for any alpha between zero and two, and alpha is usually set to one.  

The first part of the score pushes the model to be diverse. If all the generated samples are the same, the model gets penalized. The second part pushes the model to be accurate, making predictions close to the actual observation.  

Calculating the energy score exactly is tricky, so we use a Monte Carlo estimator instead. This practical version is called the energy loss. To build it, we draw N candidate samples from the generative head at each step.  

Our setup uses a conditional Gaussian posterior instead of mapping a token chunk to a fixed point. This allows us to draw M target samples from this posterior, which helps reduce the variance in the energy loss.  

The final energy loss combines these candidate samples and target samples to compute distances between them. Each distance is raised to the power of alpha, which is typically one. The energy loss is calculated as two divided by the product of N and M multiplied by the sum of all distances between target and candidate samples. Then, subtract one divided by the product of N and N minus one multiplied by the sum of distances between all pairs of candidate samples.  

In practice, N is set to eight and M is set to one hundred. Using a small N keeps training efficient, while a large M reduces loss variance with almost no extra cost.  

This training objective is flexible because it only needs the ability to draw samples from the generative head. It doesn’t require complicated internal structures, letting us design simple and efficient models. The distance used is the Euclidean norm, and the alpha power is applied to each distance before summing.

narration: The generative head is built from L residual MLP blocks. These blocks take an initial noise vector called epsilon zero, which is the same as epsilon, and turn it into a final output vector. Each block starts by combining the current representation with a hidden state using two linear layers. This step mixes the information from the current state with the hidden state. Next, a SwiGLU layer is applied. This layer has an intermediate dimension of d, which controls how much the representation can expand before being compressed again. After the SwiGLU, a residual connection adds the original input of the block to its output. This helps the model learn better by keeping some of the original information. The process ends with a linear layer that changes the representation to the target dimension l. This final layer maps the refined noise into the output vector, which is called Z sub i. The whole process uses residual connections to help the model learn more effectively by allowing gradients to flow through the blocks more easily. The intermediate dimension d controls how much the SwiGLU layer can expand the representation before it is compressed again. The number of blocks L determines how many times the noise is refined before reaching the final output. The target dimension l defines the size of the output vector. This structure allows the generative head to gradually transform the initial noise into a meaningful output.

narration: The method is called variational regularization, and it is used to create a robust latent space by changing from a deterministic autoencoder to a variational one. The encoder now outputs parameters of a diagonal Gaussian distribution, called mu and sigma, instead of directly mapping an input chunk to a vector z. The latent vector z is sampled from the Gaussian distribution defined by mu and sigma. A new objective term called KL divergence loss is added to the total loss function, which penalizes the encoded distribution for deviating from a standard normal prior. The total loss function is a weighted sum of the reconstruction loss and the KL divergence loss. The hyperparameter beta balances the two objectives, and it is set to one thousandth. The KL divergence loss is calculated using a specific formula that involves the sum of terms related to sigma squared and mu squared. The formula includes negative signs on the log of sigma squared and a constant term, and positive signs on sigma squared and mu squared. The variational objective prevents the encoder from using arbitrarily precise or large magnitude values in z, which helps create a smoother and more regularized latent manifold suitable for generative modeling. Each of these terms is summed across all dimensions of the latent vector. This encourages the encoder to produce latent representations that are close to the standard normal distribution, ensuring the latent space remains structured and smooth. The beta value controls how much emphasis is placed on the regularization term compared to the reconstruction loss. By using this method, the model learns to generate more consistent and meaningful latent representations that are easier to work with in generative tasks.

The paper introduces two dropout techniques to make the autoencoder more robust. First, dropout is applied to the latent vector z before it goes to the decoder. The dropout rate is fifteen percent. This forces the autoencoder to learn a redundant representation, making it more resilient to small errors from the generative model. 

Second, dropout is applied to the input tokens. Fifteen percent of the tokens are randomly masked. This is similar to the Continuous Bag-of-Words approach. The autoencoder must infer the masked tokens from their context, which enriches the latent vector with semantic information. 

These dropout methods are only used during the autoencoder's training phase. They are turned off when training and using the continuous language model. The autoencoder processes chunks of four tokens at a time. Each chunk is represented by a latent vector with one hundred twenty-eight dimensions. 

The encoder learns a posterior distribution where the standard deviations converge to approximately zero point three. When sampling the latent vector, Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of about zero point three is added to the predicted mean. Despite this noise, the decoder still achieves token-level accuracy over ninety-nine point nine percent. 

The resulting vector representation is both high fidelity and robust. It provides a strong foundation for training Continuous Autoregressive Language Models, or CALM.

The algorithm is called Likelihood-free Temperature Sampling. It takes a base sampler for an implicit discrete distribution and a target temperature between zero and one. It returns a sample accepted with a probability proportional to the original distribution raised to the power of one over the temperature.  

The algorithm has two main stages. The first handles the integer part of the reciprocal of the temperature. The reciprocal of the temperature is calculated, and its integer part is taken. Then, the base sampler is used to draw that many independent samples. If all of these samples are the same, that sample is kept as the result for this stage. If not, the process restarts from the beginning of this stage.  

If the fractional part of the reciprocal of the temperature is zero, the sample from the integer part is returned immediately. Otherwise, the algorithm moves to the second stage, which handles the fractional part.  

In the fractional part, a loop begins. A new sample is drawn from the base sampler. If it matches the sample from the integer part, the process returns that sample. If it doesn’t match, a uniform random number is drawn. If this number is less than the fractional part of the reciprocal of the temperature divided by the loop counter, the process restarts from the beginning of the integer part. Otherwise, the loop counter increases by one, and the loop continues.  

The loop counter increases each time the loop runs without restarting. This ensures that the probability of restarting decreases as the loop runs longer. The algorithm is designed this way to adjust the sampling process based on the temperature, allowing for more or less diversity in the samples depending on the value of $T$.

Posterior collapse happens in variational autoencoders when some parts of the hidden space stop helping with reconstructing the input. These parts collapse completely to the standard normal prior, which is the default distribution the model assumes. When this happens, those parts no longer carry useful information for reconstruction. Worse, they act like pure noise, creating a chaotic signal that messes up the training of downstream models like language models.  

To stop this, the authors use a method called KL clipping. This changes the training objective by setting a minimum value for the KL divergence loss for each part of the hidden space. The KL divergence measures how much the model's learned distribution differs from the standard normal prior. Normally, if a dimension collapses, its KL divergence drops to zero. But with KL clipping, the loss for each dimension can't go below a certain threshold.  

Each dimension’s KL divergence is computed separately. For every part of the hidden space, the model calculates how much it differs from the standard normal prior. Then, the modified KL divergence loss is calculated by adding up the maximum of a threshold value and the actual KL divergence for each part of the hidden space. The threshold value used in this work is set to half. This means that even if a dimension’s KL divergence would normally be zero, it’s treated as if it were half.  

This method ensures that every dimension of the hidden space contributes to reconstructing the input data. By forcing each part to stay active, the model avoids posterior collapse. The hidden space becomes more useful and structured, which helps downstream models learn more effectively. The threshold value is chosen to encourage participation without overcomplicating the training process.

However, this approach misses the quality of the remaining tokens in the chunk. So the authors improve this by extending the Brier score to n-grams, called Brier-n. Instead of looking at single tokens, Brier-n evaluates how well the model predicts sequences of tokens, like pairs or triples. In this version, each n-gram is treated as one single outcome. The Brier score is then calculated for these n-gram sequences. To combine the results across different n-gram lengths, the authors use a composite metric called BrierLM. This metric takes the geometric mean of the Brier-n scores for n equals one through four. The geometric mean ensures that all n-gram lengths contribute equally to the final score. For each sequence, the geometric mean is calculated first, and then these are averaged across all sequences. Finally, the BrierLM score is scaled by multiplying it by one hundred, placing it on a more familiar zero to one hundred range. This makes the score easier to interpret, where one hundred represents perfect prediction and zero represents complete failure. The goal is to sample from a distribution with a specific temperature, but the model only gives a sampler, not probabilities. This means we can’t use the usual method of scaling logits. Instead, we need a way to simulate temperature sampling without knowing the actual probabilities. The solution is a rejection sampling method that works with just the sampler.

The key idea is that repeated sampling from the same distribution can simulate raising the distribution to a power. For example, if the temperature is one over an integer, the target distribution is the original distribution raised to that integer. To achieve this, we draw that many samples and accept them only if they are all identical. If they’re not, we reject the whole set and start over. This ensures the accepted samples follow the desired distribution.

For any temperature between zero and one, we break one over the temperature into an integer part and a fractional part. The first stage uses the repetition method for the integer part. The second stage is more complex and uses the Bernoulli Factory theory to simulate a biased coin flip with a success probability equal to the original distribution raised to the fractional part. This requires an iterative process.

A sample is accepted only if it passes both stages. If it fails at any stage, the whole process restarts. This method guarantees that the samples follow a distribution where the original distribution is raised to one over the temperature, divided by a normalization constant. The CALM framework uses an autoencoder to learn a direct mapping between a group of K discrete tokens and a continuous vector. This autoencoder has two parts: an encoder that turns tokens into a continuous vector and a decoder that turns the vector back into tokens. The encoder starts by turning each token in the group into an embedding, then processes each embedding with a feed-forward network. These K hidden states are then flattened and compressed with a linear layer to create a single unified representation. This representation goes through another feed-forward network and a linear projection to create the latent vector z. 

The decoder works in reverse. It starts by transforming z with a linear layer and a feed-forward network to get a hidden state. This hidden state is expanded to K times its size and reshaped into a sequence of K hidden states. Each of these states is processed by another feed-forward network and then projected to vocabulary logits using the same embedding matrix used for the encoder. The tokens are then reconstructed by choosing the token with the highest logit value for each position. 

The autoencoder is trained to minimize the reconstruction error using cross-entropy loss across all K token positions. This means the decoder must predict each token in the group accurately. The autoencoder is efficient, using a small latent vector of ten dimensions and a hidden dimension of five hundred and twelve. When grouping tokens in groups of four, it achieves high-fidelity reconstruction with over ninety-nine point nine percent accuracy. Its design is simple and lightweight, making its computational cost nearly negligible compared to a language model.

The model starts with a discrete token input, which is a key part of the CALM system. The first idea was to take the latent vectors from the previous step and project them into the Transformer’s hidden dimension using a linear layer. But this didn’t work well. The model had trouble understanding the meaning behind those compact vectors.  

To fix this, the system uses discrete tokens instead. During training, the input for each step comes from the K tokens generated in the previous step. To keep things efficient, an input compression module is used. This is a two-layer MLP that takes the K embeddings and combines them into a single input representation.  

At inference, during step i, the model takes the previously generated K tokens, embeds them, and compresses them using the same MLP. This compressed version becomes the input to the Transformer. The Transformer then outputs a hidden state, which is used by an energy-based generative head to predict the next continuous vector.  

Once the continuous vector is predicted, it’s passed through the frozen decoder of a pre-trained autoencoder. This step reconstructs the next K discrete tokens. These tokens then become the input for the next step in the process.  

This setup lets the model work with discrete tokens, which are easier to handle and more efficient than the compact latent vectors. It also creates a feedback loop that connects the continuous and discrete parts of the system. The paper introduces two dropout techniques to make the autoencoder's latent space more robust. The first applies a dropout rate of fifteen percent to the latent vector z before it goes to the decoder. This forces the model to learn a representation that can handle small errors from the generative model downstream. The second method applies the same dropout rate to input tokens by randomly masking some of them. This is similar to the CBOW method, where the model learns to predict masked tokens from their context. This helps the latent vector capture more meaningful semantic information rather than just token indexes. Both dropout methods are only used during the autoencoder's training and not during the language model's training or inference.

The method is called variational regularization, and it changes a standard autoencoder into a variational one to make the latent space more robust. Instead of mapping an input to a single vector z, the encoder now outputs two vectors, mu and sigma, which are the parameters of a diagonal Gaussian distribution. A new term is added to the loss function, called the KL divergence loss. It measures how much the encoded distribution differs from a standard normal prior, which has a mean of zero and identity covariance matrix. This term encourages the encoder to produce latent vectors that are close to this standard normal distribution.  

The total loss is a weighted sum of the reconstruction loss and the KL divergence loss. The weight is controlled by a hyperparameter called beta, which is set to one thousandth. This value determines how much the regularization loss influences the overall training.  

The KL divergence loss is calculated using a specific formula. For each element in the distribution, it involves the sum of terms related to sigma squared and mu squared. The formula is negative one half multiplied by the sum of one plus the log of sigma squared, minus sigma squared, minus mu squared. This formula ensures that the encoder avoids using very precise or large magnitude values in the latent vector z.  

By doing this, the latent manifold becomes smoother and more regularized, which is better for generative modeling.

By using this method, the model is forced to use all parts of the hidden space for reconstruction. By using this method, the model avoids having parts of the hidden space that act like random noise. This makes training more stable and helps create a more useful hidden space. For each dimension, the KL divergence is calculated separately. Then, if it is below the minimum value, it is replaced with that minimum. These clipped values are summed together to form the total KL loss. This ensures that every dimension contributes to the training process.

The energy loss is a training objective built using the Energy Score, a scoring rule that measures alignment between predictions and observations through sample distances. The Energy Score compares two types of distances: between samples from the predictive distribution and between those samples and the ground truth observation. 

The first part of the Energy Score encourages diversity by penalizing predictions that are too similar or overly confident. The second part encourages fidelity by driving predictions to be close to the ground truth observation. 

The exact computation of the Energy Score is intractable, so an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator is used as a practical loss function called the energy loss. To compute this, eight candidate samples are drawn from the generative head at each step. These are called model samples. 

To reduce variance and stabilize training, a hundred target samples are drawn from the conditional Gaussian posterior. These are called target samples. The final energy loss is calculated using both the candidate samples and the target samples. 

The energy loss formula includes two main terms. The first compares distances between each target sample and each model sample, and these are summed together and multiplied by two divided by the product of N and M. The second compares distances between all pairs of model samples, and these are summed together and multiplied by one divided by the product of N and N minus one. 

The number of model samples affects training cost, so a small number like eight is used to maintain training efficiency. Drawing target vectors from a known Gaussian posterior has negligible overhead, allowing for a large number of target samples to reduce loss variance. 

A key advantage of the likelihood-free training objective is its flexibility. It only requires the ability to draw samples from the generative head. This allows for minimal constraints on the internal architecture of the generative head, enabling simple and efficient designs we explore next.

The algorithm is called Likelihood-free Temperature Sampling. It generates samples from a distribution with a specified temperature. The input is a base sampler for an implicit discrete distribution and a target temperature between zero and one. The output is a sample accepted with a probability proportional to the original distribution raised to the power of one divided by the temperature. 

The algorithm first calculates an integer part of the reciprocal of the temperature. Then it calculates a fractional part, which is the difference between the reciprocal of the temperature and the integer part. 

In stage one, the algorithm draws a number of independent and identically distributed samples equal to the integer part. If all the samples drawn in stage one are the same, that sample is kept as the result of stage one. If they are not all the same, the process restarts from stage one. 

If the fractional part is zero, the result from stage one is returned immediately. 

In stage two, the algorithm enters a loop where it draws a new sample from the base sampler. If the new sample matches the result from stage one, it is returned immediately. If it does not match, a uniform random number is drawn between zero and one. If this number is less than the fractional part divided by the loop counter, the process restarts from stage one. Otherwise, the loop counter is incremented and the process repeats. 

This method allows for temperature control without explicitly calculating likelihoods. The integer part ensures multiple samples are drawn and checked for consistency. The fractional part introduces a controlled randomness, allowing for fine-tuning of the sampling process. The loop in stage two ensures that the final sample is accepted with the desired probability.

The Brier score is a theoretically sound measure, but it is difficult to calculate directly for CALM because it needs the full predictive distribution P. Instead, we can use an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator that doesn’t require likelihoods. It only needs samples drawn from the model.  

The uncertainty part of the Brier score is the sum of P(x) squared over all x. This can be thought of as the chance that two independent samples from P are the same. To estimate this, we use an indicator function that is one if two samples from P are equal, and zero otherwise. This gives an unbiased estimate of the uncertainty part.  

The accuracy part of the Brier score is P(y), which can be estimated using a single sample from P. The estimator is an indicator function that is one if the sample equals y, and zero otherwise.  

To create a practical estimator for the Brier score, we combine these two parts. We take two samples from P. For each sample, we check if it equals y. Then we subtract an indicator function that checks if the two samples are equal. This gives an unbiased estimate of the Brier score using just two samples from the model.  

This estimator allows us to evaluate CALM’s predictive abilities without needing to calculate likelihoods. It uses simple comparisons between samples to approximate the Brier score directly.

The original method evaluates next-token prediction by generating two latent vectors at each step and decoding them with a frozen autoencoder’s decoder. It then calculates the Brier score using only the first token of each chunk. But this ignores the quality of the remaining tokens in the sequence. To fix this, the authors introduce Brier-n, which computes the Brier score over entire n-grams instead of just single tokens.  

In Brier-n, each n-gram is treated as a single outcome. The indicator functions used in the estimator reflect this by considering the entire n-gram as one atomic event. This change ensures that the evaluation captures the quality of longer sequences, not just individual tokens.  

To form an n-gram, the model takes the first n tokens from the generated chunk. For example, if n is three, the first three tokens make up the n-gram. The Brier score is then calculated for this whole group, not for each token individually.  

To create a composite metric, the authors take the geometric mean of Brier-n scores for n equals one through four. This combines the performance across different n-gram lengths into one value. The final metric, called BrierLM, is then scaled by multiplying it by one hundred. This scaling moves the range from zero to one to a more interpretable zero to one hundred.  

The formula for BrierLM is one hundred multiplied by the product of the four Brier-n scores, each raised to the power of one quarter. This ensures that each n-gram’s contribution is balanced in the final score. The approach follows conventions from other n-gram-based metrics like BLEU, making it familiar to those used to evaluating language models with such scores.  

At each step, two latent vectors are generated. These are then decoded to produce the chunk of tokens. The method ensures that both the single-token and multi-token aspects of the model’s output are evaluated, giving a more complete picture of its performance.

The CALM framework uses an autoencoder to learn a direct mapping between a group of K discrete tokens and a continuous vector. This autoencoder has an encoder and a decoder. The encoder takes a sequence of K tokens and maps them to K embeddings. Each embedding is processed by a position-wise feed-forward network. These K hidden states are then flattened and compressed by a linear layer to create a unified representation. This representation goes through another feed-forward network and a linear projection to produce a latent vector z. 

The encoder is designed to be context-free, meaning it processes each token chunk independently of its surrounding sequence. This simplifies the computation and makes the model more efficient. 

The decoder starts by taking the latent vector z and transforming it with a linear layer and another feed-forward network to get a d-dimensional hidden state. This hidden state is expanded by a linear layer to Kd dimensions and reshaped into a sequence of K hidden states. Each of these states is passed through a second feed-forward network. Then, they are projected to vocabulary logits using the same embedding matrix used for the input. Finally, tokens are reconstructed by choosing the token with the highest logit value for each position.

The autoencoder is trained to minimize the reconstruction error using cross-entropy loss across all K token positions. This means the model learns to predict each token in the input sequence based on the latent vector generated from that same sequence. The model is effective and efficient, achieving over ninety-nine point nine percent token-level accuracy when grouping four tokens with a latent vector of only ten dimensions. The encoder and decoder have a shallow architecture with a hidden dimension of five hundred twelve, making their computational cost very low compared to a language model. This makes the autoencoder a lightweight and powerful tool for high-fidelity reconstruction.
